I don't know how long we had been pacing the walk in this fashion, when Zamba cocked her ears. " What is it?' I asked her gently. She glanced quickly into my face and wagged her tail, then put her ears back and whined. I listened anxiously. "And presently a full sweet woman's v.oice began to sing—to vocalise. It seemed to come from the sweep before the door. There was nothing odd about it, nothing unusual. I thought a vagrant artist was singing on the chance of gaining pence, but that her voice was superior to most of the class—in fact, I never neard a better on any stage. Sometimes the sound came nearer, some- times it drifted farther off, as if the songstress were mov- ing up and down before the house, to see if at any window there were signs of life. No words were distinguishable in the song; runs, trills, and sorrowful single notes of exceeding beauty followed one another, melodiously in- deed, but with no regard to order—at least, I have not known a composition approaching that in structure. It carried me away. I listened and listened till my cigar went out, and listened still to the enchanting strains, now rising, tow falling, as I imagined the woman ap- proached or retired from the terrace. div.head: -dr.\ THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1886/ FACTS & FANCIES
div.p: -dr.\ THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1886/ FACTS & FANCIES

Who will venture to say that the women or the Far West are not economical? A young married lady of Madison, Wis., who is very fond of her hus- band, has concluded that a box of cigars will be a very nice Christmas present for him, and, accord— ingly-, has purchased the gift and concealed it from view in a bottom drawer of the "spare bureau." But she cannot help intimating to her lady friends what a shrewd bargain she had made. " Why James always pays ten dollars a box for them, and I got these for one dollar and fifty cents." Unhappy James, he little knows what Christmas has in store for him.

Among the superstitions connected with Christ- mas Eve are the following :—The bees sing in their hives; the oxen may be found on their knees in adoration of the new-born Saviour; bread baked on Christmas Eve never grows mouldy. THE cmusT3Lis TREE Where grows tile Christmas tree— The green, deep-rooted Christmas Tree? By what brave toil, in what rich soil, Can spring the blooming Christmas tree? Is it from prairies broad and deep, Where future harvests softly sleep, - And flocks of acres, far and free, Lie level as a waveless sea? Or is it where the breeze-skein twines Between the lofty plumage pines? Or where sweet stealthy Languor roves Among the Southland orange groves? Or blooms it best 'mid city homes, With Wealth's unnumbered spires and aotnes. Or is it where, through changeful day, rhe mountain shadows creep and play, And swift a gleaming sun-flood rides Along the tall cliffs dappled sides? • High grows the Christmas tree

The sweet, love-planted Christmas tree— Where'er extends the hand of friends ; Wherever ,ll2ljztlcaressings be. What bears the Christmas tree— The bright, rich-fruited Christmas tree? What gather they, expectant-gay, Who throng around the Christmas tree Leaves picked by love-instructed art Froiri off ON. brangia of the heart; Fruits culled from every tree and vine Where zephyrs fly and sunbeams shine Whate'er can brighten to our gaze The trembling dawn of childhood days; Whate'er can feed more clear and high The flame of youth's expectant eye; Whate'er can make more richly good The blood of man or womanhood, Or bid old age look smiling round. At gems of earth-joy newly found; • Whate'er can say: "while strength endures, My life has love and help for yours."' Rich glows the Christmas tree, The heart-protected Christmas tree— With tokens dear that bring more near God's earth-lent love to you and me.

MISS FOLLY'S CHRISTMAS.
It was the week before Christmas, and Miss Polly Pritchard sat alone in her little room, diligently at V,

So far, it had been a hard winter, with th-, ground all iron-bound with cruel frost; the river clad in steely-, links of ice, the sky full of snow, and wind, and tempest. But Miss Polly was very comfort.• able iii the little red farm-house, of which she occu- pied one wing, the other being rented out to Farmer 6ribbage and his wile. There was always a cheer- ful lire of logs blazing on the open hearth always a plant at the window, and a cat purring on the rug. "To be sure, it's rather lonely," said the little old maid to herself," never to have a soul to speak to. So she sat here on this gray winter's afternoon, singing seine half forgotten song, and plying her busy needle, when Mrs. Gribbage, the farmer's wife, Caine in.

" Dolls, I declare!" she exclaimed, looking at the boxes on the table. And as her quick eye fell on the ,work in Miss Polly's hand, she added: " And, as true as I live, you're a-dressite " Yes," said Miss Polly, colouring a soft, autum- nal pink. "For the toy shop? " said inquisitive Mrs. Grib- bage. "Well—no! " acknowledged Miss Polly. “They are for the little girls in the orphan asylum. They don't have any one to think of their Christmas, you know! "

" Well, I declare! 7 reiterated Mrs. Cribbage. "Why there's eighteen of 'em. You don't meau to say that you're dressin' eighteen dolls? " "Yes," said Miss Polly, in deprecating tones. "Ilumph ; Well, I just came in to tell you that I'm going up to Miss Georgietta Fullerton's to tea." • "Are you ? " said Miss Polly. Mrs. Cribbage nodded complacently. "Didn't they askljoit?" said she. Miss Polly shook her head. " Well, it's your own fault," said Mrs. Cribbage, not without asperity. " Look at that old faded, turned dress of yours. Miss Georgietta Fullerton is very particular about her dress. lid now that she is engaged to be married to the minister—" ' Miss Polly gave the least preceptible start at these words and asked: " Is she engaged to be married to him? " "So folks say," complacently answered Mrs. Cribbage. "And I don't suppose he could have made a better match. Miss Fullerton is an excellent housekeeper, and has got a little money of her own. And t is high time there was someone at the parson- age to keep those four noisy children in order." And Mrs. Cribbage sailed away in her rustling silk gown and red plumed hat, leaving Miss Polly alone with her dolls.

The parson sat alone, also, that gray, threatening December afternoon in his little study, with a heap of sermon paper in front of him. .He had sat down to write his Christmas sermon ; but, somehow, the .ideas refused to come. There was a general aspect of forlornness about the room which the poor man realized, but could not explain. "It's all very uncomfortable," said Mr. Mellen to himself, biting thoughtfully at the feather end of Isis quill pen. "And somehow I always feel it more at Christmas time than at any other. Hear those children scream! One would think they might play without snaking quite in much noise. But they are not managed as they were when poor Isabel was alive. I suppose lam not a good disciplinarian, or perhaps I should have them in better training. Really, I don't know but that the good ladies in my congregation are right, and that I ought to—" " Get married again !" Robbie Mellen's shrill, little voice uttered, 3ust at this moment. " Oh, I like that ! That's a pretty note! Our father get married again! Nonsense, Bell, someone has been cramming you! " "J3ut it's true," retorted little Bell, full of indig- nation, ',and you iliedu't laughs. I heard old Mss Grampus say 'so to Mi Collyer, last week, when they all thought I was asleep on the bed, at Sewing Society—what papa was going to marry again." " Who was it? " breathlessly demanded Janie, a tall girl of eleven. "The lady, I mean! " "They didn't say," Bell answered: • "Miss Georgie Fullerton, I bet!" shouted Bobbie. "o,.l.wouldn't like her for a mother? "
" Who would you like?" raorted Janie scorn- fully._ _

"0, I don't know: " answered Robbie. " Not her, anyhow! She sco-w:ed at me one day when I stepped on the train of her dress. And I heard her say, 'Clumsy boy to her sister." "And she was very right," didactically obserTed Janie. "You arc a cnnosy boy, Rob." "Perhaps," said John, " it's Mrs. Bricknor, There's a stunner for you! Ain't she always dressed like the Queen of Sheba ? "I can't bear Mrs. Bricknor," said Bell. She laughs too loud, and her false teeth don't fit, and I don't think she likes little boys and girls. She looked real cross at the Church pie-nic when we had them funny games, and told Mrs. Fenwick that she didn't think children ought to be allowed to malce so much noise."
"I'll tell you who does love children, though!" suddenly exclaimed Janie. " And I love her, too, and I wish papa would marry her. Miss Polly Pritchard! "

" What, that Miss Polly that has the blue Mal- tese cat, and the red cardinal bird?" said Robbie. "Well, it ain't a bad idea. She gave me some bread and jam, the night I got lost, blackberrying, on the hills, and told me such a nice story about Fortunatus and his Purse, when I was resting on her sofa."

"Yes, and what do you think? eagerly struck in Janie. "She's dressing eighteen dolls, now, for the poor little orphan girls in the asylum, and she has bought eleven jack-knives for the boys; because she says all children ought to have a Christmas." "She's a trump!" declared Robbie, pounding both hands down upon the table. declare, I've most a mind to marry her myself! But look here, Janie, ain't you going to help a fellow with these long. division sums, before papa calls us in to recite?" And Atien the noise of all four talking together drowned the sense of what they said, and Mr. Mel- len, smiling, to himself, 'pushed back his pen and sermon paper.. _ _

"Out- Of the mouths of babes and sucklings," he said, mildly. "Who knows but that these little ones' voices have been sent to guide my footsteps aright? It was a sweet and gracious idea, that of preparing a Christmas for the little homeless ones who have no parents to take tender thought for them: I think I will go out and quiet my troubled meditations with a walk! "

And his walk led him to the little red farm-house in whose wing Miss Polly Pritchard sat deligently at work over the eighteen dolls. The parson was a sensible, straightforward man, who comprehended none of the sinuous wiles of society. He knocked at the door and walked in; All looked cosy and comfortable there, from the big geranium in the window and the Maltese cat on the rug to the shaded lamp and the work-basket beside the prim little spinster. "So these are the dolls for the little waifs and strays of humanity, eh ?" said the parson, looking kindly at the maiden lady. "Yes," said Miss Polly. ", But I don't know how you heard anything about it, Mr. Mellen. It was to be a profound secret."

"I will keep it most profoundly," said the parson. "You see," blushingly explained Miss Polly, "I am fond of children, and it's a real plea- sure to do anythinr, for the little things. I've often thought I 51100171 like to adopt a child." "Miss Polly," said the parson, bluntly, " that is the very business I have come to you about. What do you say to ndopting. four! " "Four! " repeated Miss Polly. 'Yes,!' said the parson. "Mine! And theh father thrown into the bargain. What do you say, Miss Polly? Will you marry me?" "I —l'm afraid lam not good enough," said Miss Polly, with a little gasp, as if the tide of unexpected happiness was surging up into her very throat. "If ever there was a good Christian, Polly, you are one," said the parson. "Or else," putting his hand lightly upon the tiny heap of dolls, "you never would have taken all this pains for Christ's orphan little ones. Only say 'Yes,' Polly. That is all I want." And Polly said : "Yes." Mrs. Cribbage was quite incredulous when she came home and heard the news. "I thought it was to be Georg.Tietta Fullerton, sure enough," said she. "But hew ever came Mr. Mellen to think of 'you? " "I am sure I don't know," said Miss Polly, with humility. to, like the old-time fairy stories, our tale ends. " And they lived happily ever after." For Mrs. Mellen was a model step-mother, and the four young rebels at the parsonage loved her heartily. This was Miss Polly Pritchard's last Christmas in loveless solitude. For when the next Christmas came he was the happy little mistress of the parsonage.

SELF-DENIAL.—The secret of all success is to know how to deny yourself. . . . If you once learn to get the whip-hand of yourself, that is the best educator. Prove to me that you can control yourself, and I'll say you're an educated man; and without this all other education is good for next to nothing.—Mrs. Oliphant.

HELPFULNESS.—Whenever a full mind meets an empty Eine, it is a call to teach, not to scoff. When refinement encounters roughness, it is a call to influence, not to shun. When a higher nature comes in contact with a lower one, it is a call to lift up, not to thrust down. Ho Maketh you to differ that you may be instrumental in lessening that difference.

MENTAL DIGESTION.—Facts are to the mind the same thing as food to the body. On the due digestion of facts depends the strength and wisdom of the one just as vigour and health depend on the other. The wisest in council the ablest in debate, and the most agreeable companion in the commerce of life, is that man who has assimilated to his understanding the greatest number of tacts.—Burke. -- FISHING FOR COMPLIMENTS.—UW no stratagems and devices to get praise. Some inquire into the faults of their own actions or discourses on purpose to hear that it was well done or spoken, and without fault. Others bring the matter into talk, or thrust themselves into company, ad intimate and give occasion to be thought or spoken of. These men make a bait to persuade themselves to swallow the hook till by drinking the waters of vanity they swell and burst.

CRITICISM.—Don't be critical • whatever you do never set up for a critic—in private life, in the domestic circle, or in society. If you don't like anyone's nose, or obcis to anyone's chin, don't put your feelings into words. People are not all made alike or to suit one another's taste, recollect that. . Take things as you find them, unless you can alter them. Continual criticism of the conduct of this one and the speech of .that one will make home the un- happiest place under the sun.

PICKLED SPRATS.—This is an excellent mode of per. paring sprats, and very economical, forming as it does a highly piquant adjunct to bread-and-butter for supper or luncheon. Cleanse the fish—the small sprats will do equally as well as the larger sort—remove the head and gut, and wash them again in salt and water, dry them well in cloths, and put them into a pickling pan, in regular rows, strewing pepper, salt, and pounded mace over each layer, until the pan is almost full; cover the sprats with vinegar and water, about half and half, and bake them in a slow oven. They may be eaten as soon as cold, and must always be kept covered with the liquor. They improve with keeping.

A NOVEL Wonx-BASKET.—Quite an effective and often- times very handsome scrap or work-basket may be made of the discarded high hat of some. of the male members of the family. The crown is covered smoothly with silk, satin, cretonne or other preferred goods, and a wide band of velvet ribbon is arranged around its base and fastened in two stiff loops under a gilt, silver, or other slide. The brim is covered wit 4 the material put on quite full, and the lininF is also put in with a pretty fulness, the upper edge being finished with a tiny frill: The colours may be decided by the taste of the maker, and all one colour may be shewn if desired. The words " scrap-basket " or the initials may be embroidered er painted on the band. Montltly Review. s•-• • •-' ! •

REMOTINTING A PHOTOGRAPH.—Removing a photograph from a card is an exceedingly delicate operation, as the photo is likely to tear with the least pulling. If the following directions are carefully carried out, however, no difficulty will be experienced: Soak the picture in very bgt water, then take the photo in the left hand, andovith the right thumb, bend slowly and easily backwards one corner of the cardboard, and it will probably at once roll off by itself. If it does not readily come off, soak it a minute or two longer, and try again. Never take hold of the photograph itself to remove it, or it is certain to tear , and spoil; but always press the cardboard away from the photo. After the picture is removed, Ooze it between two pieces of blotting-paper, and then subject the \Owlet to pressure, taking care that it is placed straight, and. not crumpled up, and then leave till nearly dry. Before doing this, remove any traces of gum or mucilage by , washing.

SLOW EATING.—SIow mastication is of the greatest im- portance if we would live in health and avoid the horrors of indigestion, with the thousand and one ills, physical and mental, that follow in its train. Take time to eat if you would be happy. Take time to eat if you would be well. Teach your children to do so, and explain to them the reason why. A word or two spoken to a child in a quiet and reasonable Strain will qften make a very deep and lasting impression. I have a letter before me, from which I will make .an extract : "lam 17 years of age," says the writer. "and have very few teeth, but my appe- tite and digestion are good, which I attribute. to care.kl feeding. I have found by experience 1,130 0313,415 fib of food, whether dry or moist, should not be MA0,444/42„ts until reduced to a pulp and mixed with the saliva." -Let me draw the reader's attention to the words whether dry or moist." The aged but healthful writer does not allow even moist food to pass at once into the stomach. He is right. But is it not the common practice to bolt such food? Take, for example, a supper of porridge and -bil milk, or well-boiled hominy and -ow lolls do most people take to eat such a meal? And mina this is a most wholesome one. Why, about five minutes. Can they wonder that it disagrees, that it creates acidity and eructations, flatulence, and all sorts of discomforts, not the least disagreeable of which are restless nights and nightmare dreams.—Cassell's Magazine.

J AMES FRANCIS THOMAS lived in Fontnetrynydd, U. near Pontypool, Monmouthshire. He was twenty-three years of age, living with his mother, a widow. Borne eleven years before, then a mere boy, he went to work in a coal pit as a miner, in order to assist his mother in rear- ing her family of little children, Soon, however, the little fellow broke down in health, but the necessities of the family seemed to require it, and he continned to toil in the mines, suffering all the time from the effects of indiges- tion, an agonising symptom being asthma, in such a troublesome form that the poor boy was unable to lie in bed. Working through the day, and resting as best he could in an arm chair during the night, naturally under- mined his constitution. Year by year his health grew worse, until at last rheumatism came with all its dreadful agony. One joint after another got swollen and inflamed, so that he was obliged to stop work. In this sad plight the now young man was confined to toe house for two long years, suffering all mortal could endure. One physician I after another was called upon to treat his complaint,. I but with no benefit, for the poor fellow contieued to grow worse and worse.. Hoping to find some means of relief, a et nsultition of doctors was held, when it was decided that organ'e disease of the heart existed in an incurable form, and that medical aid amid not afford relief. He was given up to die. These years of expensive medical treatment had exhausted the little savings of his mother, and they had no money to buy even the necessaries of life; but a fond xn ether never gives up in despair. There was one spark of hope left. Some one had told her of a remedy that hed cured so many cases—even when as hopeless as this one seemed to be—and the mother's love went out for her dear boy. But how to get the medicine was the question. Their money was entirely gone. The boy had a new pair of trousers that he had been too ill to wear, and the mother rea- soned within herself, "[f the boy is to die he will not , need them, so I may as well pledge them for medicine, with an effort to save his life." Strange as it may ap- peitr, the bottles of medicine produced at the chemist's shop at Pontypoot, with the money obtained at the pawnbroker's, effected a cure in this hopeless else, which had been pronounced incurable. But it is only jtist to say that it the chemist had known of the wants of the family the medicine could have been ob- tained without a visit to the pawnbroker. It is now early four years since this took piece, and the young James Francis Thomas has beau able t) 1Q1421:( occupation ever since, and is in the enjoyment of excellent health. Of course he never had organic disease of the heert, as was supposed. The palpitation, rheumatism, and asthma, ware mere symptoms of the real disease, which was dyspepsia, or indigestion, for which the remedy was specially adapted. THE BULGARIAN SITU ATI ON.—RU SSI A.'S DETER- MINATION.—GRAVE STATE OF AFFAIRS, - ST. PETERSBURG, SATURDAY.—The Russian Government is determ'ned to uphold the candidature of the Prince of Mingrelia for the throne of Bulgaria and to reject absolutely the pretensions of Prince Ferdinand of Saxe- Coburg. The Bulgarian Government declares that the delegation, in offering the Bulgarian throne to Prince Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg Gotha, were acting solely on their own initiative and without previous reference to the Govern- ment. _ _ _

BERLIX, SUNDAY —Yesterday and to-clay there has been a marked tendency in diplomatic circles here to regard the situation as very grave indeed, and the impres- sion is general that the outlook has grown worse since Fri- day, and that the slightest incident may precipitate serious

events. VIENNA, MONDAY NIGITY.—The air is again full of war- like signs and sounds. So far from the rejection of the German Army Bill by the Reichstag Committee being in- terpreted as affording some guarantee that peace is reason- ably assured. the prevalent opinion is that the rebellous can- duct of the majority may go some distance towards bringing on the crisis that there is not the slightest doubt Germany wishes to avoid. SOFIA, MONDAY.—Great"disappointment is felt here at the result of. the interview between Count Herbert Bis- marck and the Bulgarian deputation. It appears that after the delegates had explained the situation to Count Herbert, he recommended them to adviss their government to accept the Russian candidate for the Bulgarian throne—viz., the Prince of Mingrelia, who, in his opinion, was a responsible and acceptable person. THE OPEttATIONS IN BURMA.II.—IMPORTANT

MURDER OF FRENCH SEAMEN ON THE SOMALI COAST. PARIS, WRDNRSDAY.—The " Temps " to-day publishes a letter from Aden, dated the Bth inst., giving particulars of the massacre of the boatswain and seven of the crew of the French war vessel Pingouin by the Eessah Somalis at Ambad.

IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. A meeting of the Warrington branch of the Irish National League was held in the League Hall, War- rington, on Sunday afternoon, to hear an address from Mr. S. Reeves, of Liverpool. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. M. Chambers, who made a few introductory remarks. —Mr. WHITEHEAD proposed" That we tender to the members of the League of the Cross our hearty appreciation of the services which, in the interests of unity, they have made in waiving their claim to hold a demonstration on St. Patrick's Day, and in return we pledge ourselves to be ready on all occa- sions to assist them by every means in our power." (Cheers.) Last year, he said, the celebration ended somewhat in a fiasco, as a counter demonstration was held in one of the public schoolrooms. He hoped that Irishmen would all unite and assist the National League, because it was the motive power of the Irish political party in Warrington. On the success of the League depended the next election in Warrington, so far as Liberalism was concerned. The League numbered 300 members, but, considering the number of Irishmen in the town, it should num- ber 500. (Cheers.)—Mr. BURN, in seconding the reso- lution, said that now or never Irishmen through- out Warrington should stand to their guns. (Cheers.) —The resolution was passed unanimously.—Mr. D. DONNELLAN proposed the following resolution : "Resolved, that we express our entire approval of the plan of campaign' now being so successfully carried out in Ireland, and beg to tender our hearty thanks to those of our Irish leaders who, at the risk of personal liberty, stand in the gap between the starving down-trodden tenantry and the cruel, heartless landlords." All the Acts that had disgraced history, he said, from the penal code down to the present day, had been in force in Ireland. The law in that country was .being carried out by partisan judges—whose characteristics were anti-Irish and who were selected from the greatest enemies of the Irish race—and by packed juries. Laws in Ireland were made to suit the landlords, and Irish landlordism and its laws were the .most barbarous in creation. It was no wonder that the greatest English statesman living said that English law in Ireland was an engine of wholesale corrup- tion against the Irish people. What respect. could they have for such laws? None—and none was deserved. (Cheers.) Irishmen in Warrington and the world over were justified in protesting against such things. (Cheers.)—Mr. WHITEEEEAD seconded the resolution, which was passed without a disen- tient.—Mr.- REEVES, in commencing his address, said that the last time he stood upon a Land League platform was in support of a resolution demanding the release of John Dillon—(cheers)—who was then in prison suffering from ill-health, and now he was on a National League platform to protest— in addition to giving his views as an Unglish demo- erat —to protest on behalf of all the democrats of England against the steps that had been taken by the Government during the last week in arresting the men who had been doing their duty to their constituencies and their country, in order to pre- 'vent the Irish people suffering the pangs of famine and hunger likely to approach them in the coming winter. (Cheers.) The question of the trouble in Ireland was not a sentimental one. At the present day any man not blind or stupid could see that the whole end and aim of the English Government in Ireland was to make it possible for landlords who had no right there to gain impossible rents. It was for this reason that the plan of campaign or- ganised and developed by Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien was calculated to bring about the ends sought—mot only by making it impossible for land- lords in Ireland to obtain impossible rents—but it was a step by which a death blow might be dealt at landlordism in Ireland altogether. He was not there to say what was fair or unfair rent in Ireland, because it was his opinion that the land of Ireland —or any other nation—belonged to the people of such nation—(cheers)—and any rent which went into the pockets of an idle, useless, and cumber- some class was an unfair rent, whether it was a penny or a pound. (Cheers.) If there was any sur- plus left in the agricultural workers' hands it should not go into the pockets of the landlords, but to the national exchequer, not of the English, but of the Irish nation. (Cheers.) When famine was in Ire- land—when Irishmen were compelled to ask for as- sistance cargoes of food stuffs and cattle were leaving Ireland to be sold in Eng- lish markets to pay rents to English land- lords. • The people were not able to feed themselves from the products of their own land, but had had to hand it over to the landlords. It was this that compelled him to be in favour of the plan ot campaign, not as a final end, but as one step in the direction of securing to the:lrish people their inherent rights in the land of Ireland. it WaS not just now so much a question of Home Rule as of bread and butter for the Irish. He rejoiced in the present agitation because it showed that there were men who were determined, come weal come woe, that Irish liberty should not be sacrificed. It was to themselves, and themselves alone, that they mist trust in the coming fight. The man who to- day had confidence in the Liberal party was depend- ing upon a rotten reed. The Only fault he ever had to find with Irishmen was that they were twofond of forgetting and forgiving. It was only five years ago since the Liberal party were just doing what the Conservative party was doing now, and were the Liberals in power to-morrow it was just as possible they would do the same. Home Rule became practicable only when the Liberal party foiind they could not carry on the Government of the country without the Irish party. Give them a thumping majority, and Home Rule might go to the winds, without circumstances arose in Ireland which made the continued Government of Ireland by England impossible. They must rely on themselves, backed up by what help they could get from the independ- ent democracy of this country. The English Gov- ernment of to-day was that of a class, and the English democracy suffered from pretty much the mrne evils as Ireland (cheers). It was in England, as in Ireland. Ireland was dominated by a small class of landlords and they in England were domin- eered over by a'larger class of landlords and capital- ists. Re believed that it was only by the combina- tion of Englishmen. and Irishmen in England that the democratic question in England would be fought out, and, when the Irish question was settled, Irishmen would have time to help their English fellow workmen. It. was the battle of the • people in both cases, and the people would win. (cheers).—A few remarks having been made by Mr. W. Stirrup and Mr. John Chalmers, a vote of thanks was passed Mr. Reeves for his address, on the motion of Mr. Whitehead, seconded by Mr. Donnellan, and the proceedings concluded with a.. vote of thanks to the chairman.

------- - - - MANDALAY, SUNDAY. Brigadier-General Low has stormed the quarters of Boshwav, who, after some sharp fir- ing, retreated into the jungle with his followers. The rebel leader's camp was captured by the British. KYANICIIYAT, SUNDAY.— General Roberts reached Bhamo on the 15th. He arrived here to-day, examined all the river posts, and arranged the details of the expedition against Wuntho, the chief who is still afield. A thousand men will form the main body of the expedition, which is to start in January. General Roberts has settled the site of Its entrenched position at Bhamo, where there will be a per- manent garrison of 1,300 soldiers. Thera is no news of the attitude of the Chinese at Yunnan, but a missionary reports that the tr: lers are suspicious of the interference of the British. Every effort is being made to reassure them. MANDALAY, MONDAY.—Daring the past week small columns have been working in all directions, and have met with but little resistance. The process of disarming is being carried out, especially in the Yan and Tsagin dis- tricts. 394 firearms are reported to have been captured or surrendered during the past week. Boshway having fled from Najeb, that position has been occupied by General Low. EGYPT.—THE RELIEF OF EMIN BEY.

The Paris offices of the New York Herald on Monday received the following telegram from Dr. Wilhelm Junket, dated Zanzibar, December 20, II a.m. :—" An expedition for the rescue of Emin Bay is most urgent. Routes are now practicable if a strong and thoroughly well-organised expe- dition be sent. I myself think it would be best to send a strong expedition under the command of Stanley, as there will be fighting. I shall reach Cairo January 5.,2 ITALY.—WAR PREPARATIONS.—CARDINAL JACOBIN'. The Italian Minister of Marine, speaking in the Chamber of Deputies, on Monday, in support of an extraordinary credit of 25,Ci00,000 lire, half of which is to be applied to the military and the other half to the naval service, said that enrich vet remained to be done to assure the complete maritime de-fence of Italy, but the improvement which had already been effected gave the Government confidence in the great services that could be rendered by the navy in case of necessity. Rosm, MONDAY..—.Cardinal Jacobin', Pontifical Secretary of State, yesterday tendered his resignation to the Pope on the ground of ill-health, and although his Holiness refused to accept it, the question of appointing a successor to the Cardinal is being discusssed at the Vatican. AMERICA.—THE IRISH NATIONALISTS.—RRIBERY TRIAL. PHlLA•ort.pma, IIIoNDAY.—The Irish Nations! League held a meeting at Philadelphia on Friday last, at which a liani Of 3)1309 dollars was subscribed to the Irish fund. The second trial of Alderman McQuade on charges of bribery and corruption concluded on Monday. The jury found him guilty, and he was sentenced to seven years' imprisonment, and ordered to pay a fine of 5,000 dollars. FRANCE.—THE SUEZ AND PANAMA CANALS

CAIRO, SATURDA.Y.—The commission representing the Suez Canal Company to-day concluded the arrangements with the Egyptian Government for widening the cane'. By Ms scheme, to which the signaturei of the parties will pro- bably be affixed on Monday next, the width et the coal from Port Said to the Bitter Likes is ,;to be 44 metres, and thence to Suez 65 metros. A Paris telegram of Saturday says that at a meeting of the Geographical Society, M. de Lesseps again declared that thle Panama Canal would be open for traffic in 1839. He added that there would not be satilcient time for the con- etructice of locks, which woald be reads later on.

Mr. de Lessens is said by the papers to have stated at a banquet that 140 million francs more were necessary to complete the Panama Canal. FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT. On Wednesday night, at Syndal I Colliery, West Houghton, near Bolton, two colliers, names Jesse Chadwick and Edward Gradwell, were killed. The rope attached to waggons on the incline leading to the pit eye loosing the waggons, the deceased, along with others, were ascending the incline, and were caugat by the waggons and instantly crushed to death. The others es- caped by taking refuge in a manhole. The men leave widows and families. _ _ _

FOIIIS CHILDREN SUFFOCATED.—An inquest was held at Carrick-on-Suiron Monday on the bodies of four persons who bad died from the effects of an escape of gas. On Saturday night a yanman, named Cornelius Hearne, retired to rest with his wife and family consisting of six children. Early on Sunday morning, owing to the non-appearance of any of the family, a forcible entrance was made, and the whole of the occupants of the house were found lying in their beds apparently dead, while the fumes of gas filled the dwell- ing. Medical aid was at ones obtained. Four of the children were found to be dead, and Hearne and his wife were so seriously ill that they were conveyed to the work- house infirmary. It was ascertained that a gas main had burst from the effects of the intense frost. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1886:
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1886:

THE CAMPBELL DIVORCE CASE. The hearing of the Campbell Divorce case was resumed on Saturday before Mr. Justice Butt. Sir Charles Russel continued his speech on behalf of Lady Cohn Campbell, contending that the evidence of the servants was unre- liable. In the Queen's Bench Division on Saturday, application was made on behalf of a private person for a rule nisi for a criminal information against the London Evening News on the ground that it had published a libel. The atleged libel consisted in the lengthy reports which the evening Conser- vative organ named has given of the medical evidence in the Campbell case. The object of the applicant was to try the question whether it was permissable to publish full re- ports of Divorce Court cases. The Judges refused to grant a rule, while evidently sympathising with the object of the applicant, and suggested that another course should be taken. The Campbell divorce case came to an end on Monday night. Sir C. Russell resumed at the opening of the sit- ting his address en behalf of Lady Colin. He dealt in the most unsparing manner with the witnesses for Lord Colin. and described Lady Colin as "a lady by instinct and by education." With regard to the Duke of Marlborough, Sir Charles said he was not there to offer any defence of his general conduct, but it was the fact that men whose antecedents were notoriously bad were received in society. On this point, it will be remembered, Lady Colin and her mother made some curious observations. Both agreed that the Duke's "divorce court reputation "was no bar to their friendship for him. Sir Charles advised the jary not to pay too much attention to " Pecksniffian morality." The right hon. and learned advocate having concluded, Mr. Justice Butt followed. He dealt out severe censure to Lord Colin, and described him as being ready to pawn his honour for money. The learned Judge accused Lord ' Colin's witnesses of" gross falsehoods," and said that the conduct of Lord Colin in trying to get his wife arrested in Paris was outrageous, dishonest and infamous. His lord- ship conchsded his summing up at thirty-seven minutes past six, and the jury retired. Shortly after nine it was rumoured that the jury had sent a note to the judge, and almost immediately after Lord Colin Campbell re-entered the court and took a seat beside Mr. Finlay. Immediately following him came Lady Colin Campbell, Lady Miles, and Mrs Neptune Blood. The jury returned into court punctually at 13 minutes past nine, and were succeeded by the judge. Mr. Justice Butt intimated that he had received a com- munication that there was no possibility of the jury agree- ing. The Foreman said the jury were agreed upon Lady Colin Campbell's petition on the charge of adultery against Lord Cohen.

The Judge replied that their finding on that might be taken, but it would be a great misfortune if there were no other verdict for the other petition. There were co-respond- ents. Were they, he would ask, agreed as to any one of them? —4O _ _

The Foreman said they were differing as to whether Lady Colin Campbell had committed adultery or not, and there did not seem to him to be any chance of their agreeing. The Judge wanted to know if they were agreed that Lady Colin had committed adultery with any of the co- respondents. The Foreman said they could not find that they had committed adultery with Lady Colin, unless they could find that she bad committed adultery with all of them. He offered to mention the division amongst the jurors, but the judge declined to allow this to.be mentioned. On his lordship's suggestion the jury then again retired, to see it there was any possibility of their arriving at a de- cision.

The jury again retired at twenty minutes past nine o'clock. On returning into court at thirteen minutes past ten, The jury found that Lord Colin Campbell had not com- mitted adultery with Mary Watson, and that Lady Colin had not committed adultery with any of the co-respondents in Lord Colin's-petition against his wife. The verdict was received with some applause in court. At the same time the jury expressed strong disapproval of General Butler's conduct in not coming forward, and stated that he was indirectly responsible for the delay there had been in coming to a decision. Lady Colin Campbell and her friends left the court im- mediately on conclusion of the trial by the staircase leading to the private corridor. As she passed out her face flushed with satisfaction. Her ladyship received congratulations from many of those standing in the well of the court. A large crowd had for a considerable time been collected in front of the principal entrance from the Strand to the Royal Courts of Justice awaiting the result of the trial, and a considerable number of police wire stationed there to pre- eery° order. There was some cheering when the verdict be- came known, and the people soon after dispersed.

, At the Westminster Police Court, on Tuesday, Thomas J. DAlar,. described as a clerk, was brought up on remand, charged with attempting, by means of a letter, to extort he sum of 100 from Lord Colin Campbell.. Lord Colin de- posed to the receipt of the letter, the contents of which tv_re to the effect that unless the sum named was forwarded to a given address, a communication of a surprising nature would be made to Sir Charles Russell. The prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court, bail being refused.

in the Divorce Court, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Batt for- mally gave judgment. On the application of Mr. Inderwick, hit lordship dismissed the petition against Lady Colin. Mr. Inderwick asked that full costs should be allowed her lady- ship in reference to both petitions, and some converation took place, in the course of which Mr. Searle, on behalf of Lord Colin Campbell, was ordered to pay £l5O costs in the action which his wife brought against him, and be was also ordered to pay the full costs in the actions which he'brought against his wife. the Duke of Marlborough, Captain Shaw, and Dr. Bird. No application was made for General Butler's costs.

I past and present deplorable condition of the land I question. • At the Cork police Court, cit Monday, Dr. Tanner, ' M.P., and Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., were charged with assaulting District Inspector Milling on the ' occasion of the disorderly proceedings in that city on the night of the 2nd December, when "Tim Hurley" arrived in custody from the country for trial at the assizes and received a welcome from a section of the populace. It was not contended on behalf of the prosecution that the assault was much more than a technical one, and counsel for the defence argued that the meeting which the police dispersed was a lawful assembly. The magistrates were divided in opinion, with the result that the case was dismissed. Mr. O'Connor's charge against Mr. Milling was then withdrawn. • Mr. William Redmond, M.P., was on Monday served with a summons to answer a charge arising out of his advocacy of the "Plan of Campaign." In the Land Court, on Monday, Judge Boyd made an order to " attach " certain tenants who had resolved not to pay their rent unless a specified reduction was made. _ _ _ _

A party of " moonlighters " attacked the house of Mr. Goggin, farmer, Ballinprior, near Tralee, on Saturday night. Mr. Goggin was absent at the time. On his return home the men fired twice at him, but missed their aim. Subsequently they fired upon several policemen whom they encountered, wound- ing one of them in the leg. At Armagh, on Tuesday, a man named John Proc- tor, aged 25 years, was stabbed whilst standing at his own door, and died almost immediately. Two men, named Gartland and McKenna, fowl pluckers by trade, have been arrested on suspicion of being the murderers.

It is stated that the preliminary steps have been taken by Messrs. O'Brien, Dillon, Sheehy, and Har- ris to institnte actions against the authorities for illegal seizure. On Tuesday, in the Queen's Bench, Dublin, Mr. Healy applied to fix an early day to argue whether an appeal lay for the decision of the court, requir- ing Mr. John Dillon, M.P., to give sureties for his good behaviour, and in default, to be imprisoned for twelve months. Judge O'Brien refused the applica- tioe, stating there was no appeal. The fortnightly meeting of the League was held on ruesday in Dublin. Mr. Harrington, M.P., an- nounced that £540 had been received from the British Isles and £5,000 from America.—Mr. Dillon, M.P., who presided, said the Irish party meant to carry on their policy, no matter what the Govern- ment might do,—Mr. Healy said the Government, as in .Lord Spencer's time, took no action till the "plan of campaign" was three months started to keep the people in their farms. Nothing more in- solent was attempted than the efforts of thQ ciovorn- ment to put down the movement.

div.head: CRISIS IN IRELAND.
div.p: THE CRISIS IN IRELAND.

PROSECUTION OF IRISH LEADERS, &c. On Saturday the Irish Executive issued a pro- clamation stating that the movement called "the plan of campaign" is an unlawful and criminal conspiracy by whatever name it may be known or by whatever means it may be carried out; that everyone who promotes and joins therein will ex- pose himself to prosecution: and that all money, re- ceipts, books, and documents given or received for the purpose of the said conspiracy are liable to be seized, and the person found in possession of them to be arrested and brought to trial. On Saturday, in the Dublin Police Courts, an ap- plication was made by the Crown solicitor for a summons against Mr. J. Dillon, Mr. W. O'Brien, Mr. W. K. Itedinond, Mr. M. Harris, Mr. D. Crilly, and Mr. D. Sheehy to appear in the Dublin Metropoli- tan Police Court on the Thursday, to show cause why they should not be sent for trial, and as notice has been served upon the four leaders who were re- manded at Loughrea on Thursday week that they will not be required to attend, it appears that the proceedings are to be transferred from Loughrea to Dublin.

Mr. Parnell, M.P., and his mother, Mrs. Delia Par- nell, have arrived in London, and are staying at the Euston Hotel. Mr. Parnell has been seriously ill from a sharp gastric attack with complications, but is now much better. He has been gaining strength rapidly during the last few weeks, and his medical adviser is confident that with care he will be able to take part in the work of the session by the opening of Parliament. Mr. Parnell does not propose to express any opinion as to the "Plan of Campaign" at present, as he is desirous first of going to Ireland and having an opportunity of consulting with the gentlemen responsible for its organisation and working, whom he has not seen since the close of last session. Ile also wishes for further informa- ticn than at present in his possession with regard to various matters before he speaks publicly on the subject. Mr. Parnell was not aware that the "Plan of Campaign" had been devised or was going to be proposed until he saw it after its publication. Mr. W. O'Brien was the chief speaker on Sunday, at a National League meeting at Longford. He declared that the Government never intended to bring him and Mr. Dillon to trial, but that the whole procee- dings were a fraud and a sham, the Government hoping that before they could obtain the verdict of a jury they would have succeeded in suppressing the national movement by proclamations and by their arbitrary conduct. Captain Vandeleur's tenants met on Saturday at Kilrush to ascertain the final determination of their landlord as to the demand for a reduction of rent. No communication had been received from the land- lord. The walls of Kilrush have been placarded ' with ejectment processes by Captain Vandeleur against his tenants, who have resolved to adhere to the plan of campaign; and the Nationalists have replied with a poster calling upon the people of Kilrush to become "soldiers of Ireland under the ; banner of the National League." Mr. J. Deasy, M.P., addressing a Nationalist meeting at Killarney, on Sunday, said he believed , the Government intended to introduce a Coercion ; Bill, but prophesied that the Gpvernment would , F not remain long in office •if it attempted anything ; of the kind. Mr. Harrington, M.P., called upon the ; people to set their faces against the outrages that ; had made their country so notorious. On Saturday, the closing day of Munster Winter Assizes, terms of imprisonment were passed upon prisoners who had been convicted of moonlighting offences, posting threatening letters. and of being in. unlawful possession of arms. In the course of the day Tim Hurley was again put upon his.trial on a charge of having dynamite in his possession with a felonious intent. The jury returned a verdict of acquittal. It is stated that during these assizes 47 cases have been tried and as many as 463 witnesses examined. div.head: SHOCKING CHILD MURDER NEAR
div.p: SHOCKING CHILD MURDER NEAR
BOLTON.

On Saturday afternoon a shocking murder was committed at Aspull, near Bolton, the wife of a col- lier named France killing her infant daughter Ellen, six months old, by almost severing the head from the body with an ordinary table knife. She then absconded, but afterwards gave herself up to the Bolton police. The France family, embracing hus- band, wife, and five children, resided in that part of the township known as the " Gullett." The father and eldest boy are employed at an adjacent colliery, and were at work when the crime took place. About twelve on Saturday morning Mrs France visited her mother, who lives close by, having with her then the unfortunate child. After a brief stay Mrs France returned to her own house, and sent the children who were at home out to play. Nothing more was seen or beard of the mother and child for an hour, about which time a neighbour, entering the house, found blood stains about, and on her cal- ling in others a search resulted in the finding of the body of the child on one of the beds upstairs with the blood-stained knife beside it. Search was made for the mother, and two Aspull constables tracked the woman across country for miles, losing trace at Westhoughton. Later on Mrs France gave herself up to a constable in the Bolton borough force, stat- ing that she had killed her youngest child by cut- ting its throat. She was handed over to the county authorities, and when charged admitted the crime.

On Monday, the woman France was brought up at the Bolton County Police Court and formally charged. She appeared in the dock with a shawl thrown over her head, and stared about in a vacant fashion. "Sergeant Lomax stated that after receiv- ing information he proceeded to the residence of the prisoner in Lower Gnllett, Aspull, where he found the child with its throat terribly cut. He set out in pursuit of the mother, whom he tracked across the fields to Westhoughton Station, where she had taken the train to Bolton. He subsequently received ' her from the borough police. On his formally charging prisoner, she replied "That's true."—On the Magistrates' Clerk asking whether she had any- thing to say, the prisoner said "It's true enough," , but appeared quite 'Unconcerned. She was then re- manded pending the inquest.—The woman has been ; in a di3sponding state of mind for some time, and ' has been attended by Dr. M`Loughland, of Aspull, who advised her husband, a collier, to keep a strict watch on her actions. The murder was committed with a shoemaker's sharp-pointed knife, which has been found, covered with blood, and which was kept in the house for the purposel of peeling pota- toes. It is believed that the woman, about whose insanity the police have now not the least doubt, meditated killing both her youngest child and a daughter three years old, as she had taken them both upstairs, and only sent the elder one down when a neighbour called to her from below. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Edge, the coroner for the district, held an inquest at Aspull on the body of a child named Ellen France. The Coroner said that the mother was mot present, as she was very weak, and he did not think it advisable, as the evi- dence would have to be repeated before the magis- trates. It 'transpired from the evidence ,that the woman was insane with regard to religious matter& The Coroner said it was for the jury to return a ver- dict of "Wilful murder against Mary France." They had nothing whatever to do with any defence which might be raised elsewhere. The jury at once returned a verdict in accordance with the coroner's suggestion.

div.head: LIFEBOATS CATASTROPHE.
div.p: THE LIFEBOATS CATASTROPHE.

i The coroner's inquiry into the capsizing of the Southport and St. Annes lifeboats on the 9th of 1 December and the loss of twenty-seven lives was concluded at Birkdale on Saturday. The verdict was one at • death from misadventure, and coupled with this the jury made a number of recommendations as to the means to be used to save life from wrecks in the future. The two most important suggestions were that there should be two boats on the station instead of one, and that there should be a properly organised double crew in place of the present system of volunteer crews. The report of Sir Digby Murray and Captain the Hon. H. W. Chetwynd on their inquiry into the recent diaster to lifeboats off Southport was on Monday presented to the Board of Trade. The in- spectors are of opinion that the loss of life was attributable to the Southport boat never righting after she capsized. There was evidence that she. made several attempts to do so; but always fell back" again. They think her failure to right was occa- sioned by the anchor having been let go, and also to the number of men holding on round and undex the boat, though the former of the two causes would probably be sufficient to account for the casualty. The inspectors refer to the evidence that some of the crew remonstrated with the coxswain for keeping the boat broadside to the sea, and and remark that, considering that he was a man of great experience who had rendered good service in the past, they are not disposed to give much importance to the allega- tion. In the case of the St. Annes boat, as none of the crew have survived, any opinion as to the cause of the disaster must be purely.hypotheti- cal. The inspectors regret to have to state that they found that the coxswain was physically unfit for the performance of so arduout and difficult a service, as he was ill with consumption and was not expected by his medical man to last beyond the spring. The coxswain was the only one in autho- rity present when the boat was launched and despatched, and therefore no one alive is responsible either for the coxswain or any of the men proceeding ,in the boat on the night in question in an unfit P condition. In concluding their report the inspec- tors notice the great gallantry of the fishermen of the neighbourhood. The Committee of the Royal National Lifeboat 1 Institution on Monday passed a resolution record- ing its high appreciation of the past services of the crews of the Southport and St. Annes lifeboats, and its sympathy with the -widows and families of 1 the men who lost their lives in the heroic attempt to rescue the crew of the Mexico. The Committee decided to grant special rewards to the survivors of the Southport lifeboat crew and to the crews of the Lytham and Blackpool lifeboats, as well as the silver medal of the Institution to the coxswain of

ASSAM-1174'1012NR5% The first team of the Askam-in-Furness team visited Warrington on Satur- day, to play off their return match with the premier local team, but as the severe frost had so hardened the ground that it was as a matter ef common prudence decided not to play the game in the ordinary fashion. But in order not to entirely dissappoint the spectators by whom this match had been looked forward to with great interest it was agreed that a drawn game should be played, collaring and other things which might lead to heavy falls en the frost-bound ground to be dispensed with. This, of course, prevented anything like a test of the respectivo merits of the teams, and there- fore comments on the " points " of the game are superflu- ous. Nevertheless some very interesting play, and not a little amusementto the spectators, was the result of the encounter. The Askam club were well represented, but Warrington was short of Davies, Dillon, Jolley, Fair. Turner, and Ashton. In the end the score stood, Aekam three minors, Warrington one minor. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Very little footballing was done on Saturday, owing to the frost, and in different parts of the country important and Interesting Matches had either to be cancelled or postponed. Warrington was no exception to the rule, for Saturday was the day appointed for the return fixture between the home team and Askam. Had the weather been propitious this would probably have been one of the best matches of the season, as the visitors, so far as appearance and repute went, turned up with a splendid team. To play on the ground as it was would have been a very rash undertaking, and it was wisely decided, in order not to entirely disappoint the spec- tators of their expected treat, to play a " friendly " game under rules specially devised for the occasion. The result was an amusing game if not a very exciting one. Notwithstanding the severe weather, the match North v. South of England was brought off at Blackheath on Satur- day, when the South again scored a victory, winning by one goal and one try to two trieE, the winning point 11:.ing only notched within the last few minutes of the game.

div.head: WARRINGTON SAYINGS BANK.
div.p: WARRINGTON SAYINGS BANK.

The annual general meeting of the trustees and managers of the above institution was held on Tuesday morning at the Bank premises, Butter- market-street. The Chairman (Alderman J. R. Pickmere) presided, and there were also present Mr. W. Long (vice-chairman), Mr. S. Rigby, Alder- man J. Davies, Mr. J. 11lite (trustees), Alderman Webster, Messrs. W. Darbyshire, R. W. Francomb, Roberts, J. Cliffe, J. Hatton, T. Jolley, W. Owen, J. Morris, F. W. Monks, T. Whittle, and J. R. Young (managers), and J. E. Davies (actuary). THE MANAGERS' STATEMENT.

The Committee of Management presented the general statement of the bank for the year ending 20th November, 1886. It showed as follows :—The total funds amount to £295,734 Gs id, as under With the National Debt Commissioners on the gene- ral account £291,599 13s sd, on separate surplus fund account £7OO, and the balance with treasurer £3,434 12s 8d ; making £295,734 Os id. The total due to depositors is £203,439 17s 7d, leaving a sur- plus of £2,294 8s 6d. £7,697 13s .1d interest and £135 12s dividends on stock have been credited de- positers, and the' total amount due to them shows an increase for the year of £3,400 Os Id. 756 new accounts have been opened, and 642 closed, shewing an increase for the year of 114, the total number of depositors now being 9,584. The Committee again wish to specially point out to depositors who have more to deposit than £3O a year, and £l5O in the whole, that they may invest through the bank £lOO a year or any smaller amount, not less than £lO, in the purchase of Government stock, and the bank receives and cre- dits their ac2ount with the half-yearly dividends. The number of inVestors in stock is gradually in- creasing, and the stock register shews a balance of £5,975 or £3 per cent. consols held for depositors. At the monthly meeting of the committee the ac- count'of the bank have been examined and found correct. It is a pleasure to the coinmittee to pre- sent so favourable a report. The usefulness of the institutioncannotibe denied and h efact that the num- ber of depositors and the funds of the bank continue to steadily increase is very gratifying.. There have been as many as 15,056 transactions during the past year. The bank is now open daily from 11 to one o'clock, on Wednesdays until four o'clock, and Sat- urday evenings from six to eight o'clock, and offers every facility to those who wish to save and make' provision for times of need.—The CHAIRMAN moved that the statement of accounts be approved. Every- . thing, he remarked, was going on satisfactorily, there being an increase in the number of accounts and also an increase in the amount deposited. He be- lieved the bank was doing good work, and although there were so many accounts of depres- sion they did not seem to lose ground, but went on from year to year the same as before. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. W. LONG seconded' the pro- posal and concurred in the remarks of the chair- man.—Alderman WEBnER remarked that whatever distress there might be in the town the number of deposits did not seem to decrease. People seemed to be impressed with the urgent neces- sity of husbanding their resources to the best advantage and they evidently had every confidence in that bank.—Mr. T. JOLLEY also referred to the satisfactory position of the bank,- after which the motion of the Chairman was agreed. to.—Mr. JOHN WHITE next mOved that the report. of the Committee of Management be approved, and. that the meeting acknowledge the valuable services - rendered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the committee during the past year, and tenders its best thanks to them.—Mr: H. ROBERTS seconded the proposal,which was unanimously agreed to.

APPOINTMENTS. - -- Alderman WEBSTER moved that Major Pickmere be elected chairman, and Mr.W. Long vice-chairman of the committee, and this having been seconded by Mr. W. OWEN it was agreed to.—Mr. FRANCOMB moved,,and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, that the following gentlemen be requested to form the Com- mittee of Management for the enSuing year ; Trustees, chairman,vice-chairman, Memrs. C. Broad- bent, P. Monks, J. Davies, S. Rigby;. and T. Litton; managers, the Mayor (Dr. Mackie), Messrs. T. Jolley, W. Darbyshire, W. Owen, J. P. Young;, James Mor- ris, ex-Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and the Rev. J. Yonge,—The CIIAIRMAN said they regretted the ab- sence of the Mayor, and they could only hope that he would soon so-far recover as to be abla to render them some assistance. (Hear, hear.) The• Chairman likewise alluded to the presence of Mr. S. Rigby, and said that the Warrington Savings Mink must be a very interesting institution when a meeting in connection with it could bring Mr. Rigby so far, and especially in such weather. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was then agreed to. Votes of thanks to the chairman and viceuchair- man brought the prcceedings to a close.

reductions set up by the tenantry were perfectly reasonable and inevitable. It will be seen, therefore, that, viewed from the Irish stand-point, the Plan of Campaign has its redeeming features. It compels bad landlords to make those reductions in rent which good landlords have voluntarily con., ceded; and, as Mr. DILLON argued before the Judges, it is simply doing what Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH and General BULLER have sought to do in a more round-about way. It is altogether different, it will be seen, from the " no-rent" policy which the Liberals, when in office, were called upon to grapple with and suppress. It affects a small portion only of landlords, and as they are of the rack-renting class they can be left to fight the battle, with the Government be- hind them, without requiring that we should, like NIOBE, be all tears on their behalf. As for the Government themselves, they are reaping where they have sown. They de- liberately rejected Mr. PARNELL'S bill, which was specially designed to meet the present issue, and, as tl-ey have failed in so many cases in putting pressure on the worst landlords, they can scarcely be surprised that the Nationalists should apply the screw in another way. The struggle between the Government and the people of Ireland hn now commenced; the Tonle will fall back upon the old bad weapon of coercion, which has failed a hundred times, and will fail again. Lord SALISBURY has his opportunity, and we shall s-e what he will make of it. Meantime, Liberals who are more than ever convinced that there is only one way out of the Irish bog, must continue to make tracks towards the beacon light of Home Rule.

There has been such hard vearing in the COLIN CAMPBELL case, on one side or the other, if not on both, that no one can pretend to be astonished at the jury dismissing both the petitions for divorce. It was a matter of course, after the medical evidence with regard to AMELIA WATSON, to say that no jury would come to the conclusion that Lord COLIN CAMPBELL . had been guilty of such conduct with her as was attributed to him. The real tug of war has been as to the charges against Lady CoLIN CAMPBELL; and the evidence has revealed so much that is utterly demoralising that the public were pre- pared to believe anytl, ing and everything as possible, even where absolute proof was not forthcoming. Judge and jury are to be pitied in having had to undergo such an ordeal. It is impossible for any man, however pure minded, to listen day by day to such evidence as has been adduced in this case without, consciously or unconsciously, undergoing deterioration in moral fibre; or, to put it in another way, one cannot be steeped in pitch without being defiled. A good deal has hap- pened within the past twelve months to sug- gest that "the better classes 'S are no better than they should be; and we need not wonder that the poor of the Metropolis, who are always on the verge of starvation, should have bitter things to say of the rich when they meet in Hyde Park or Trafalgar Square. It is obvious that there is something rotten in our social system when a matron of the Upper Ten can go into the witness box and openly declare that she sees no impropriety in her daughter associat- ing with a nobleman who has been divorced from his own wife because of his running away with the wife of another nobleman. It is not sufficient to say that " society" toler- Ptes these things—so much the worse for society when it has no morality which is worth preserving. It cannot be said that any of the parties to the suits come out of it without being considerably smirched. General BUTLER showed more discretion than valour; he failed to put in an appearance, and he is told by the jury that his "conduct. is alto- gether unworthy of an English officer and a gentleman." On the assumption that he is innocent, it seems inexplicable that he should not assert his innocence on oath; for, grant- ing that he cared nothing about his own char- acter,which is a far-fetched suppositon,it must not be forgotten that the character of a lady was at stake, to whom reputation was every- thing. If he felt, however, that he could not go in the box and exculpate either ,linself or Lady COLIN-CAMPBELL, he has actec. .visely in putting himself beyond the reach of a subpcena ; and, let us add, he shows that,what- ever may be his faults, he is not entirely dead to-conscience. It will, perhaps, be thought time, after the public mind has been pois- oned with a few more such cases, to turn our attention to the law of divorce, and ask whether it would not be better to relax it in some degree. It is obvious that, if Lady COI4N had obtained a divorce from her hus- band when a judicial separation was decreed, the community would have been spared the nauseous revelations of the past three weeks. According to the evidence originally given, she had a strong case against her husband— a case which, as it seems to us, ought to fully warrant the law in saying there should not only be a separation but a dissolution of mar- riage. The trial which has just ended has been a great scandal; it is a relief to know that it is at an end; but it would be a greater relief to know that the state of the law was such that there could be no possibility of its revival.

number of purchasers which, in the main, accounts for the great improvement in our magazines. The same observation applies with not less force to the wonderfully varied supply of Christmas Cards which are to be seen on every hand. The charming vignettes which we admire arc the result, in many in- stances, of the labours of artists of no small merit who have, in the first place, been paid no small sum for the original drawing, a copy of which is placed in our hands for 6d. or 3d., or it may be a rd. We are not amongst those who are sceptical as to the ameliorating influence of art and of education generally, and we are pleased to see from the annual reports of the School of Art and of the Boteler Grammar School, that in both respects Warrington is making satisfactory progress. A shilling or two well spent in Christmas cards will do much towards brightening and beautifying homes that would otherwise be dull and cheerless; while another shilling or so spent in Christmas literature will provide that which can be passed from hand to hand, and give the reader new life by introducing him to a new world. It is a great improve- ment, at any rate, upon the reckless expendi- ture in intoxicating liquors so frequently wit- nessed at this time of the year; for cards and books are not, like beaded bubbles,winking at the brim "—" a moment seen—then gone for ever," and they do not lead to quarrels and fights, with headache, and perhaps "five shillings and costs" in the morning. Art and education are not everything, but they are a great improvement upon drink and degradation.

Lamb, of 69, Irwell-street. A lesv minutes later Mrs Lamb missed 28 front a pur•.!..: she had placed in a drawer. The girl positively deni,d tbe accusation, and there being 3 doubt in the case she was diecharg,d with a caution.
