When Mr. Lea appeared the defendant struck him twice —The Bench fined the defendant 103 and costs each case; total 395. AN EXPENSIVE LODGER AT WlDN'ES.—Robert Hodson, a " fitter," was brought before Mr. Gossage at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, charged with having on the 7th March last, and divers other days, obtained by false pre- tences, food, lodging, and money, front W. Jones, keeper of a common lodging house in Lugsdale-road. The prisoner represented that he was a pensioner, and had deposited his papers, upon which he would receive £6 lOs on the Ist April, with Inspector Wood at the Police Station. Jones, on this understanding, allowed the prisoner to lodge at Lis house several weeks, and lent him money. On the sth April the prisoner decamped, leaving a debt of £3 23„ and he was apprehended at Chester on Tuesday by P.C. Porter. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

causes of complaint they had was that their Board Schools had not been as efficiently managed as they might have been. They had not been put on a pay- ing basis, and the members thought it was a scandal to the schools that every year a deficiency had to bet made up from the pockets of the ratepayers. Mr. Handley had taken great pains in the matter of attendance, and owing to his exertions the attendance had been improved. Ths.-Jy found that the teachers were not efficiently taught, and immediately the mem- bers set to work to improve the tuition they received, and in that way the tuition would work downwards, and the children would be benefited. Mr. W. Handley expressed the opinion that the pre- sent lumber of members on the School Board were not sufficient now they had to undertake the duties of school managers, and that there ought to be an in- crease, and that the time of electioa should be at a more convenient season. Since he had been a mem- iwer of the Board he had not seen any denominational leanings on the part of any member, and he pointed out that- the present Board, which was almost t new one, wc6 not responsible for the policy now pursued. The Runcorn Board had foimerly about the worst average attendance in the kingdom, but it. had recently been increased from a little over 60 to 8o per cent on the average. He thought more school accom- modation would be wanted before long, and he had no doubt the School Boar 4 would be very glad if the Denominations would provide it and save the pockets of the ratepayers. He expressed the hope that a con- test would be avoided.
Dr. McDougall bpoko strongly about the high School Board rate, and was in favour of avoiding a contest.
Mr. Meadowcroft remarked that if rateable value was to be considered, he was the most eligible charac- ter. (Laughter.) He trusted a contesz would be avoided.

Ultimately the Nonconformists and the Church- men retired into separate rooms to ccuisider what should be done. Upon their return into the Board- room the Rev. W. Preston stated that Mr. Lightburzt and Mr. Meadowcroft had most generously with- drawn, and consequently the Church would be repre- sented by Dr. 'MacDougall, Mr Lake, and Mr. 'raison.

Mr. R. Shaw said while the Nonconformists con- sidered they were entitled to a larger representation, they were willing to be content with three represen- tatives to avoid the expense of a contest, as there was no burning question to decide. It was understood that the Nonconformists who were willinsr to withdraw were Messrs. Beckett, Frith, and liniveton ; and the constitution of the new Board will remain the same as hitherto, with the excep- tion of Dr. MacDougall, who takes Mr, Lf3o'l3 place.

A T 317011 STRUG3LE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Smith, a powerful-looking sailor, was charged with assaulting P.C. Povey while in the execution of his duty. On Sunday night the officer saw the prisoner and a woman in an unlawful position, and be arres- ted the woman. On the way to the station he was attacked by ‘hree men, and the prisoner released from his custody. The prisoner struck the officer on the eye and mouth, and the officer then seized the prisoner and a long struggle en- sued, the prisoner making ;requent use of his fists and feet. By P.C. Sutton's aid, the prisoner was taken to the police station, where it was seen that the prisoner and his captor were much exhausted. The prisoner had to be supplied with a glass of Water, and the constable could not speak for five minutes. The prisoner, who bad no defence, was fined LI and costs 78 4d, or in default a month's hard labour. A SNOWBALLER HEAVILY FINED AT WIDNES.—At Wils nes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Harper, a youth, was charged with assaulting James Bright, an elderly man, who lives in Lacey-street. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the complainant, and Mr. W. T. Husband for the defendant. It was alleged that on Sunday afternoon, as Bright was coming from his labours at the Widnes Alkali Company's works, the defendant and a number of other youths, who were in the habit of annoying Bright, assailed him with snowballs for a distance of several hundred yards. At length Bright picked up a brick and threatened to use it if rbe were not allowed to proceed quietly. Upon this Harper rushed at Bright, knocked him down, and struck him in the face and kicked him in the ribs ; and a dog was also set upon the prostrate man, who was bitten on the nose and ear. Bright was unable to follow his employment next day.— Witnesses were called to corroborate this statement.—The Bench, after hearing the defence, were satisfied that Bright had been snowballed and assaulted, and imposed a fine of 20s and costs upon the defendant. SWINE FEVE... AT WESTON.—At Runcorn Patty Sessions, on Monday. before Mr. F. Rigby and Mr. James Handley, a labourer named Thomas Whitby, who lives at Weston, was charged that he having in his possession a pig which was affected with swine fever, did unlawfully fail to report that fact to the constable of the district. The defendant pleaded guilty.—lnspector Millington stated that on the 7th in- stant he found a dead pig in the stye attached to defend- ant's house. The pig was much discoloured, and the veter- inary surgeon, after making an examination, declared that the pig had died from a very bad attack of swine fever. According to the defendant's own statements he knew the pig had been suffering six days, but be did not, report the case until the pig was dead. Notices had been from time to time posted in the neighbourhood, showing that it was the duty of pig keepers, when they found a pig suffering from any disease to report the case to the police.—The defendant said he thought the pig was only staked.—The Bench Im- posed a fine of lOs and costs Os 6d. Mr. Rigby pointed out that a penalty of £2O could have been inflicted, and as the offence was of a very grieyous character, any future cases would be severely dealt with. TILE RECTOR, OF WARRINGTON AND HIS TITHES.— On Tuesday evening a meeting of the tithepayers of Burtonwood, and the district was held at the Chapel House Inn, Buttonwood, for the purpose of receiving the reply of th e Rector of Warrington to th e Ideputation appointed by a previous meeting to wait upon him and ask for a reduction of 20 per cent. of the tithe charge. The chair was occupied by Mr. Richard Forshaw, who stated the result of an interview of the deputation with the Rector. The Rector, he remarked, stated that he was £2OO worse off this year than last, and therefore could not see his way to make any reduction. After enumerating the calls made upon him, the Rector advised farmers to rear fowls as a means of extricating themselves from their difficulties. After some discussion, it was resolved and carried that the farmers of the district do not attend the tithe audit, unless a reduction of 20 per cent. in the tithe rent charge be conceded. A further resolution to the effect that a local branch be formed in Burtonwood in connection with the Warrington Farmers' Club was unanimously car- ried.
THE PLASTERERS' STRIKE AT WIDNES. ALLEGED INTIMIDATION.

Colonel Gamble and Mr. T. S. Timmis were engaged several hours on Monday afternoon, at Widnes Police Court, investigating the charges of intimidation of workmen employed at the new public offices, by the plasterers on strike. Janes Kemp, Michael Gravey, Michael Loftus, James, and Starkey, of Liverpool ; and James Westworth. of St. Helens, were charged, under four different informa- tions with having, without legal authority, followed a num- ber Of men, employed as plasterers at the new Tawn Hall buildings, from place to place, and beset the works,; with having unlawfully and wrongfully intimidated John Evans, and with following John Evans in a disorderly manner through the streets. Mr. Pickford, barrister (iastructed by Messrs. Tyrer, Kenioo- and Co., Liverpool), appeared for the prosecutor, Mr. J. H. Johnson, slater and plasterer, Liverpool ; and Mr. Shand, barrister (instructed by Mr. William Rudd, of Liverpool), represented the defendants, with the exception of Westwoeth.—Mr. Pickford said the history of this case was the history of a dispute between Mr. Johnson ond the defendants, who were the representa- tives of the Live-nool Plasterers' Society. Mr. Johnson had a contract to pe form the lathing and plastering at the Widnes Public Offices, and discontent arose because he ac- cepted the services of some Widnes men to do the lathing at a rate of wages which was not the rate accepted by the mem- bers of that Liverpool society. The result was a communi- cation from the secretary of the society protesting against the employment of these men, and, in fact, against employ- ing any men not members of the Liverpool Plasterers' Socie- ty. Mr. Johnson did not recognise that this society had any right to dictate to him in that way, because this society, according to their own rules, only had jurisdiction for a radius of 11- miles from St. George's Hall. Liverpool. The consequence was a strike, and other men from S. Asaph, Warrington, and Widnes were engaged.—Benjamin John- son, brother to the prosecutor; John Birchall, of Warring- ton ; Patrick Kelly, Inspector Wood, and Police-constable M'Guinness gave evidence for the prosecution.—Mr. Shand contended that there had not been any case of intimidation proved, and that in persuading men to go away on payment of their fares the men were perfectly within their rights and had violated no law. Without hearing the witnesses for the defence, the Bench decided that it had not been proved that the law had been broken. Those men had come to Widnes to prevent men from working, but they had man- aged very cleverly,under the corntnand of their secretary,the defendant Kent, to avoid breaking the law. Although they might have persuaded these men to go, they had not compelled nor threatened them, nor had they followed them about in such a way as to come within the section. West- worth was the only one who had used any violence or threat, and he did not belong to the society.—Mr. Pickford asked the bench, as they did not consider there was a care against the others, not to deal with Westworth, and the magistrates agreed.—Mr. Pickford appli 1 for a case to be stated, in order to raise the question whether the facts as uncontradicted did not disclose ao offence under the section. —Colonel Gamble said the bench considered there were no facts proved within the meaning of the section, and de- clined.—Mr. Shand applied for costs, bat their worships re- fused to accede to the request.

CHRISTMAS, in its relation to literature and art, is a very different thing to what it was a generation ago. Of the making of Christ - mas books there seems to be no end, and at Christmas-tide they come to us for the most part admirably illustrated. Almost every magazine has its special Christmas num- ber, and this luxury of literature, so far from being confined, as it once was, to the luxurious classes, finds its way into the homes of tee humblest. Those who cannot afford to spend a shilling in a book may find special issues at as low a figure as one penny, and find them, too, adorned with illustrations that are not by any means to be despised. The multiplica- tion of Art Schools throughout the country has had a rapid and marked effect upon book illustration. Messrs: CASSELLS have al- ways been in the front rank in this class of work; but let anyone who has the opportunity and time turn to an old number of " Cassell's Magazine," and com- pare it with the current issue; they will be astonished at the difference--a difference which is entirely to the credit of the magazine of to-day. The fact is there has been a vast improvement in taste, in technical skill, and in methods of produc- tion and reproduction. But these things do not account for the whole of the difference. It is the extraordinary increase in the number of readers consequent upon the growth of population, and 'upon our compulsory system of education, that has enabled the great pub- lishing firms in these latter days to supply high class work at a low class price. Th,. fi cost is, of course, the great cost, and when the , sale reaches hundreds of thousands where it = formally reached thousands, it will be seen that, after all, it is the great. increase in the

WYCLIFFE DAY SCHOOL CONCERT.

On Monday evening, the annual concert of Wycliffe (Warrington) Day School, was held in the Public Hall, in the presence of a large number of the parents and friends of the scholars, and of others interested in the school. The first part of the programme was commenced with a kinder- garten song.—" Crowning the May Queen," sung by the younger children with, prettily attired, had a very pleasing appearance. The May Queen was chosen and crowned with befitting pomp, and then the children gaily plaited and unplaited the May Pole, with a grace that was, considering their juvenility, somewhat surprising. They had evidently been well trained, and, in addition, took a personal interest in the performance that was in itself almost enough to guarantee success. A short cantata by Karl Merz—" The Wandering Gipsies" —was next given by the elder scholars, a solo part being rendered with much ability by .MiSs M. Pod- more. Miss M. Perry played a solo on the violin in such a manner as to ensure her the hearty applause of the audience, and the first part of the programme was brought to a close by the scholars going through. "Musical Drill."

During an interval that ensued, the Rev. JOHN' YONGE, pastor of Wycliffe Church, said that all pre- sent, he was sure, would be sorry that, in conse- quence of a very sharp attack of illness, Mr. Mc- Minnies was unable to be with them. He was however to be able to say that Mr. McMinnies was recovering from his illness. (Cheers.) He was much better, but still not able to leave his room. In his unavoidable absence, Mr. Frank Roberts had undertaken to take the place of Mr. Malinnies. (Cheers.) Before Mr. Roberts did so, however, it devolved upon him (the speaker) to give some par- ticulars with respect to Wycliffe Day School, which he thought would not be without interest. The school was examined on November 25th and the three following days by Mr. George Syder, Her Majesty's Sub-Inspector of Schools. In the mixed department 390 children were presented for exami- nation. The subjects taken were reading, writing, and arithmetic, grammar and English literature, geography and map drawing, needlework, and sing- ing by note. The percentage of passes for the whole school was 96. For the third year in succession the school had been awarded the highest merit grant for obtaining the mark "excellent." Last year Mr. W. Scott Coward, the former inspector of schools for the district, characterised the schools as one of the best in his district. It was worthy of note that Mr. Coward's successor had confirmed this statement. The following was a full copy of this year's report :—" In tone, discipline, and instruction this large school maintains its excellent condition. In every class both teachers and children show an earnestness and thoroughness in their work pleasant to witness. The organisation and working reflect great credit on the zealous and able head master. In reading, the lower standards are rather too much addicted to pointing. Hand-writing is very good on the whole, and spelling is very accurate in all standards, except in the fifth standard, where there is a large number of half-timers and thew same circumstance may account for a lack of intelligence in this class in working problems in arithmetic. The know- ledge and intelligence shewn in the class subjects are most creditable." Two of the pupil teachers had this year gained Queen's scholarships. Sydney Jeffrey was placed 122nd on the general list of England and Wales, and Elizabeth Annie Place 552nd on the general list for females. The former was going to Borough-road, London, and the latter to Edge Hill, Liverpool. He (Mr. Yonge) had also received a letter from the headmaster of the War- rington Grammar School intimating that E. W. Coates (People's College), F. Dendy (People's College), and John G. Place (Wycliffe School) had been elec- ted to free scholarships. (Cheers.) He thought that all the friends of Wycliffe School would feel that the statement was satisfactory and encoura- ging. (Cheers.) • Mr. FRANK ROBERTS then delivered a short ad- dress. He was, he said, very sorry that the first meeting of Wycliffe School that had been held in the Public Hall should not have been graced by the presence of Mr. McMinnies. Everyone who had any connection with Wycliffe knew what Mr. McMinnies had done for Wycliffe. (Cheers.) He was certain that they all very much regretted his absence, and lie was also certain that nothing but ill health would have kept Mr. McMinnies away. (Cheers.) They had heard a good report of Wycliffe School, and they had got that report from a hard examiner, but the headmaster liked a hard exami- ner, for he then got all the more credit for a good. report. Let the people who were interested in edu- cation in Warrington understand the plain position in which they stood. In most of their towns the people rejoiced in a School Board, and he had heard some people say that it was a disgrace that the same did not apply to Warring,ton. He knew what a school Board was, for he had to pay School Board rates. He was very glad that in Warrington they .were not called upon to pay them. (Cheers.) Especially during the winter months they were a great hardship. In Warrington; they rejoiced in the voluntary system, and if the supporters of it were going to keep up their prestige they must assist voluntary schools. Some might say that they would be very willing to assist voluntary schools, but they must be satisfied that the education ()liven in them was as good as that given in board schools. He thought that after lieaing the examiner's report they would think that Wycliffe was such a school, and anyone in favour of the voluntary system could hav•dly refuse to support it. They should therefore take care that such a school did not suffer from want of funds. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the entertainment, he said he thought it was a credit to all who were engaged in it, not only to the .ee er pre sl . a young and old scholars, but also to the vocalists generally. (Cheers.) Mr. Corney and his assist- ants also deserved thanks for the able manner in which they had placed the entertainment before them. It must be a pleasing thing to the parents of the children present to see their sons and daughters make such a good display. more, Mr. SW. S. LAST week end the Government arrested Mr. JOHN DILLON, M.P., and three other Irish leaders who were engaged in carry- ing out what is known as the Plan of Campaign ; and this has been fol- followed by the formal proclamation of the Plan of Campaign itself as "an un- lawful and criminal conspiracy." It is no more than was to be expected that the Gov- ernment should take this course,after the dis- tinct expression of opin'on on the part of the Judges who called upon Mr. DILLON the oiher day to find sureties for his good beha- viour. Indeed, it would have been cowardly on the pai. of the authorities o- the CrOwil not to act up to wh they were told was not only the letter but the spirit o' the law. But having said this, it does noi, follow that we are in duty bound either to support the gene- ral policy of the Government, or to stigma- tise .hose who have been carrying out the Plan of Campaign as ‘• daylight robbers." In the first place, until Mr. DILLON was stir:en-toned, it was a moot :point NO- ether what he was doing could be regarded as ille- gal ; and now that it is pronounced unlawful it still is an open question whether the Plan is one which should r-.Adiated as immo- ral. The Anti-Vacch )rs sometimes go , the length of resisting ti ; but it is not customary to .denounce their conduct on that i account as m. :oral. What is the Plan of Campaign? It is an clganisation whereby certain of the L ish leaders take upon them- selves to receive the rents of certain tenants —the money to be th,ed as a means of resis- ting the landlo, ds ; but this is not done ex- cept where the landlord has refused to accept a fair rent—that is a rent from which a rea- sonable deduction hps o mrnade on account of the depression in agriculture. Mr. W. O'BRIEN, replying to those who have rashly condemned his action, says : it is a. ridiculous misconception of .our Plan of Campaign that it is a gigantic conspiracy against all rent in Irelan,-. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Look out for squalls—Lord Randolph Churchill has resigned his post as Chancellor of the Exchequer.
It is stated that the Tories are adding their signatures to those of certain Liberal Union- ists who are "requisitioning" Mr. Chamber= lain to address a meeting in Edinburgh. Curious—isn't it ?

The Postmaster-General has a hint to Rive to the public ; and it is this: if you want to treat the postman, treat him, but, ,` an you love him," don't treat him to intoxicating liquor, for, as things go, it is bad treat- ment.

There is an unquestionable improvement in trade in the United States. The railways are doing more business' and that means more business all round. The traffic returns show an increase for every month this year, except the first. It is about time the Britisher had a turn. The "Christmas waits" are annuals— hardy annuals—but the waits for good trade are, like the poor, always with us. --- Alexandre Jacques, who has been experi- menting in London, has broken his fast after twenty-one days' trial, owing, it is said, to some pecuniary difficulties interfering with the continuance of the experiment. Jacques has done quite right. If a man cannot keep out of pecuniary difficulties when he is living on nothing a day, he ought certainly to turn again to the flesh pots— and "specially when everything smacks of Christmas.

Cowley Schools, St. Helens, have not, like some old institutions, been left behind in the struggle for a place in the front rank. At the annual distribution of prizes, on Tuesday evening, Mr., A. Sinclair, J.P., stated that, in the Government examination in mathe- matics, the pupils had gained a larger number of certificates of merit than any elementary school within twenty miles of St. Helens. This is certainly something to be proud of.

Mr. Gladstone keeps his eyes on the Sister Isle. In a letter to a Scotchman he says: I decline all political controversies at present except one; nor is this from indifference to other matters, but because it is my belief that progress will not really be made with them until this one is out of the way." "And so say all of ps." Mr. Gladstone will enter in his 78th year on Wednesday next. " Many happy returns." The Warrington Starr-Bpwkett Buildin Society has made a capital start, and held its first appropriation meeting on Monday even- ing. Alderman Davies, who presided, shrewdly remarked that the acquisition of saving habits would tend to uproot the So- cialism which was allied to pauperism. He seemed to think it as good a thing to have a stake in the country as it is to have a steak in one's inside—this cold weather--and we dare say he is not far wrong.

A woman died at Glasgow on Tuesday through burns, resulting from the explosion of a paraffin lamp. Scarcely a week passes in London • without a death from this fright- ful cause. Mr. Charles Marvin, in a pamph- let on "The Moloch of Paraffin" says that all the cheap lamps are absolutely unsafe; in fact, he knows of one lamp, and only one, that secures immunity from danger. He thinks it is time for Parliament to intervene. " We insist," he says, "on safety lamps for the mines; let us do something to provide safety lamps for the masses."

Mr. Bromley Davenport, M.P., speaking in Macclesfield on Monday, said it was use- less to expect a reimposition of protective duties for the benefit of suffering agricul- turists. What they must aim at was the fostering of a general revival of trade, which would give the farmers more customers to buy their produce. This is too bad of .Mr. Davenport. If Tory members of Parliament begin to talk (Liberal) sense, what chance will there be for the Fair Traders.? What is the use of Protectionists crying aloud against Mr. Gladsone if they are not to be "protected" when Lord Salisbury is in office?

A Scissors-grinder, who seems to have gone from door to door, was recently brought be- fore the magistrates for hawking without a licence ; but the Bench decided that his was not a case which required one. A poor girl from Liverpool was less fortunate; she was locked up at St. Helens on :Saturday for being without license whilst hawking paper decorations for Christmas. The mother, on Monday, said she had five children to sup- port, and didn't know that she was doing wrong. The magistrates, after hearing the explanation, set the girl free. She had cer- tainly been sufficiently punished, for such a trifling offence, by being kept in gaol from Satu:day till Monday.

There has been a generous response to the appeal made on behalf of the families of brave fishermen who perished in the wreck of the Southport and St. Anne's lifeboats. The Royal National Lifeboat institution headed the list with a subscription of Lz.ooo. div.head: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

The annual distribution of prizes in connection with this school took place on Saturday afternoon. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided, and amongst those present were the Rev. George Bond (vicar of Farnworth), Messrs. Eustace Carey, W. A. Watts (head master), and A. J. Rant (assistant toas- ter). The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said he was informed by Mr. Watts, the head master, that the scholars were increasinz in numbers. The institution had now been in operation for some few years, and it was most important that everyone who could assist them should de so, because whilst the School Board gave a very elementary education, still they had no organisation for au intermediate or secondary system of education. Mr. Watts then gave some particulars relative to the school, after which Miss Shaw, of Liverpool, distributed the prizes, which were as follows :—Upper Form.—Latin: 1, Frank Mercer; 2, James Eatock. Mathematics: 1, James Bate ; 2, Charles Bate. English: 1, Frank Mercer; 2, Charles Bate. French: 1, James Bate; 2, Frank Mercer. Science: 1, Archibald kyle; 2, Charles Bate. Lower Forin.—Latin : 1, Samuel Tinsley; 2, George Griffiths. Mathematics: 1, John Clibbon; 2, Samuel Tinsley. English: 1, John Clibhon ; 2, Samuel Tinsley. French : 1, Samuel Tinsley; 2, Harold Baker. Science: 1, Samuel Tinsley ; 2, John Clibbon. Music: 1, Frank Mercer; 2, John Clibbon. Drawing— Freehand : Archibald Kyle. Geometry: Walter Albert Watts. Professor Hile Shaw (chair of rngineering, University College, Liverpool) during the afternoon de- livered an address, a vote of thanks being afterwards ac- corded both him and Miss Shaw, on the motion of the Rev. George Bond, seconded by Mr. Eustace Carey. An enter- tainment followed, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: CHRISTMA.STIDE AT RUNCORN /OD
div.p: CHRISTMA.STIDE AT RUNCORN /OD
WIDNES.

The festive season of Christmas has again arrived in the ordinary cycle of events, and it is gratifying to know that in the neighbourhoods of Runcorn and Widnes there is no reason why it should not en- joyed to the full. Athough trade is not exception- ally brisk, and the wages of the labouring classes are not at the high level they were some years ago, still it is 'fairly good, and there are brighter pros- pects, caused by the extensions in Course of erection at some of the existing works, and the establish- ment of new industries. There is no lack of em- ployment; and people can view with antici- pations of pleasul.e the displays that are made by the tradesmen. Butcher and baker, draper and tailor, all have 'decked their windows to the best advantage. The wares vended by the drapers and tailors, whilst not attracting so much attention as the edibles, were displayed in a bright fashion, and there may be mentioned Messrs. Uns- worth Brothers, High-street, who have a great variety of articles suitable for Christmas and New Year's presents; Mr. R. Morris, high-street; Mr. W. H. Rogerson. Bridge-street; Mr. S. Coventry. Church-street; and Mr. W. Blythe, tailor, High- street. In Widnes also there wee preparations on every hand for the season. Messrs. Elwood, Smith, and Co. had attractive displays of presents intended for purchasers of their teas at their establishments —Victoria-road, Widnes-road, and Mersey-road. The shop of Messrs. Unsworth Brothers, Waterloo-road, was appropriately decorated, and their wares were brightly assorted to attract attention. In fact, all the shopkeepers had made some attempt at decora- tion, and the shops had a brighter appearance than on ordinary occasions.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

The time during which persons could be nominated as candidates at the School Board election, fixed to take place on the 31st jest, expired on Monday. The nominations were as follows :—Catholic : Rev W Fennelley. Church of England: Dr MacDougall, Messrs F A Lake, E Imison. Nonconformist : Messrs J Pritchard, R Shaw, W Handley, S 0 Bec- ket, J R Frith, B Sniveton. Independent : Messrs Meadowcroft and 3 W Lightburn. With the ex- cepton of Mr R Lea, the retiring members seek re- election. • IMPORTANT MEE riNG.-A CONTEST AVOIDED.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of the candidates and their supporters was held in the Town Hall, Waterloo -road, with the object of arranging a com- promise, and thus avoiding the expenditure of about £l3O on a contest. There were present the candidates, with exception of Father Fennelley, who was repre- sented by Mr T Williamson, the Rev W Preston, M.A., and Messrs T J Mitchell, J R Digges, J Uns- worth, W Mellor, E Taylor, J Humphreys, J W Woodland, G Hewitt, T Handley, John Williams, W H Rogerson, T H Annett, and G Moss. Mr James Pritchard, the chairman of the expiring Board, occupied the chair, and explained that the meeting was called in order to ascertain whether some arrangement could be come to whereby a contest might he avoided. If this could be done it would be in the interests of the ratepayers generally, who, he believed, were anxious to avoid the expenses of a contest.

Mr J W Lightburu expressed his approval of the present representation—three Churchmen, three Non- conformists, and one Catholic—and said if these lines were adhered to he should be glad to withdraw his nomination in order to save the turmoil and expense of an election.
Mr Woodland thought a fairer proportion would be two Churchmen, two Wesley3n., two other mem- bers of the Nonconformist b9dy, and a Catholic, and he moved a resolution to that effect.

Mr 3 Unsworth said the representation should be based upon the rateable value of the constituents, and he thought the suggestion Mr Woodland had made was a very fair one indeed. As the Nonconformists were by far the largest section of the ratepayers, he thought they were entitled to a larger rePre.entation than they had had hitherto. He seconded Mr Wood- land's motion.

Mr. Lightburn remarked that he based his with- drawal on the understanding that the present repre- sentation of parties was maintained. The Church, he argued, had stood the brunt of the elementary educa- tion for years past, and he thought it strange that a proposition of that kind should be made by Mr. Woodland. The REV. W. Preston said Mr. Woodland's proposi- tioft was one of the coolest assumptions he had ever heard.—(hear, bear,)—and wished to place those who had done nothing for education on more than equality with those who had borne the brunt of the day for many years. The Church party would never assent to it. The Church party held a meeting the other even- ing, and they decided to do all in their power to carry things on the old lines, and that those ,who had done most for education should have three representatives. They asked no more and they would accept no less, if they could help it, and that the Roman Catholics shorld not be left in the lurch. He paid a tribute to Father Fennelley's abilities and labours on the School Board, and said the selection of Holy Trinity Church WIS Dr. MacDougall, and Mr. Imison and Mr. Lake were the other selections of the Chtrch party. Mr. Taylor was surprised that Mr. Preston and Mr. Lightburn should refer to.the religious question; he understood it was a ratepayers' question. The repre• sentation suggested by Mr. Woodland was certainly in proportion to the ratepayers votes as they were in the first election.

Mr. F. A. Lake said it was a pity they should fight the battle on merely sectarian lines, He had never sought to be a member of the Board, he was nomin- ated in his absence, and he left himself entirely in the hands of his party. As to the proportion of re- presentation he understood that in the past elections the church party returned three members so that it was fair to assume they would do again. Mr. S. C. Beckett remarked that in the first election there were four Nonconformists and thre Churchmen returned. Father Fennelley had no seat. Mr. R. Shaw said that if they had lines laid down upon which the Board should act, they might select .the seven members as •suggested by Mr. Lake. In the first place that the Board schools should be made as efficient as possible ; next, that they should not be competing schools against sny denominational schools—(hear, hear)—that they should not reduce the foes in the Board schools so as to compete unfairly with the existing schools; and then in the next place that the Board should consider that it was just as much their duty, after carrying out the two points he had named to do everything that was possible to make sectarian schools a success. If any applications should be made by managers of any sectarian school for increased accommodation, that it should be allowed to be done, as this would mean a saving to the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) in answer to Mr. Pres- ton, he pointed out that a :very large proportion of the money that had supported these voluntary schools had come out of the pockets of the taxpayers. (A. voice : A small proportion.) He explained that it was not by his desire that he wa3 nominated, and ex- pressed the hope that the matter would be arranged. Mr. Lightburn questioned whether the School Board had any control over the extensions of volun- tary schools, but Mr. Shaw was upheld ",.)y Mr. Annett.

Mr. Moss cordially agreed with the policy described by Mr. Shaw, and the gentlemen nominated on be- half of the Church could be trrsted to carry out that policy, and on that ground he claimed for them Mr. Shaw's support.
Mr. Inii;on said Mr. Shaw had undoubtedly put his hand on one of the weak poin's in the School Board administration of Runcorn. The Nonconform• ist members would bear him out that one of the great

div.head: LoCAL NEWS.
div.p: LoCAL NEWS.

NEW CURATES FOR RUNCORN.—The Rev. W. W. K. Ormsby, M. , Trinity College, Dohlin, and the Rev. W. Bryant, B.A. and B.Sc., London University, have been licensed as curates to the Parish Church of Runcorn. THE NEW VICAR OF RUNCORN will be formally welcomed to his parish on the Oh January. at a tea meeting to be held ia the National school. Such an excellent reputation has preceded the rev. gentleman that the desire to inset and hear him is widei.pread. BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT AT WIDNES.—On Tues- day evening an entertainment was given by rhe members of the Hatchinsen-street rrimitive Methodist Band of Hop.', when a capital programme of voc il and instrunieutal music. recitations, and dialogues WAS gone through. ST. JOHN'S MUTUAL BENEFIT SOCIETY. RUNCORN.—The accounts for the year have been wound up, and it dividend of 9s 3d per triemlier was decicved. Mr. W. Leach has been appointed president for the ensuing year, and Mr. J. L. Longshaw and Mr. F. Hewitt secretary and treasurer respectively. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. Mr. G. A. Danbv, clerk to. Widnes School Board,on Thursday had several persons before the magistrates on charges of not Bending their children regularly to scihool. The cases were proved by arr.-la:Jac° officers Davies, Joynson, and Rowe, and the tented flue of 53 was imposed in each case. INQUEST AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Ship Inn, Heath- road, on the body of the infant son of FreAerick Pilling, of 10, Sutton-street, Runcorn. The child was born early on Saturday morning, and on Sunday morning it was found dead in bed lying on the mother's arm. Verdict, "Found deed." CHARITIES AT liaterox.—The annual meeting of the trustees of the Halton charities was held on Tuesday, at the Norton Arms, when there were present the Rev. John Lock- wood (chairman),Mr. C. L. Evans, representing Sir Richard Brooke, tart., and Mr. John Smith, of Dutton. Sixty cases were dealt with, the amount dispensed being upwards of £2l, besides various gifts of coal. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES.—A fraternal visit was paid to the "Good Samaritan" Lodge I O.G.T.' Widnes, on Monday evening, by the members of the "Prosperity of Runcorn" Ledge. A miscellaneous entertainment was given by the members of the Rnncorn lodge, which com- prised several temperance glees, titc.. The members of the Runcorn lodge were afterwards entertained to supper. CAMDEN WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.—At the last weekly meeting of this society Mr. A. Harrison contributed a paper on "The Jesuits." There was a large attendance, Mr. H. Randle presiding. A discus- sion took place, which was taken part in by Messrs. H. D. Kitto, J. Moulton, J. David Jones, W. Carroll, and J. B. Clarke. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Harrison at the close, on the motion of Mr. W. J. Shore, seconded by Mr. S. C. Beckett. MISCELLANEOUS CONCERT AT OVERTON.—The annual concert of the Frodsbam Endowed School was held in the school-room, Overton, on Tuesday evening, when an in- teresting and enjoyable programme was gone through by the scholars, under the guidance of Mr. Hutton, the assis- tant master, consisting of choruses. songs, recitations, cornet solos, a laughable dialogue entitled "Lodgings to let,' and the ballad, "Little Cock Robin." Mr. B. A. Rigby accom- panied each of the choruses and songs on the organ. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. The annual sermon on temperance was preached to a good con- gregation on Sunday evening last by the Rev. J. Thornley, of Sheffield. A collection was taken on behalf of the Band of Hope. ' On Monday evening the young members of the Band of Hope were given a tea in the schoolroom, whilst the adults were charged for the repast. Subsequently the children gave an entertainment under the presidency of the Rev. R. Burden, and during the evening addresses on tem- perance topics were given by the Rev. J. Thornly, and the Rev. E. Hall, the pastor. FREE MEALS ON CHRISTMAS DAY.—Mr. S. Stringer, hair- dresser. Victoria-road, who took such a prominent part in organising free dinners for the hungry children of poverty stricken parents during the severe weather last winter, has arranged for a free dinner to be given to the "little chicks" in the infant school at Simm's Cross Board school, on Christmas Day. Potato pie and plum padding will be the bill of fare: More will not be met with denial, as in the case of Oliver Twist. At the United Methodist Free Church a number of the scholars have collected sufficient subscriptions to give a large number of childrea a hearty breakfast, and this will be done on Christmas morning. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The usual fort- nightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday afternoon. Lieut-colonel Ashton occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner Messrs. Weir, Aaron, Parr, W. Whitlow, Hadfield, BrarNeth, Lowe, Hewitt, J. Whitlow' Knowles, Percival, Pickering. H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy- clerk). The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Adams) sent a report, in which it was stated that he had investigated out- breaks of measles at Halton and Stockton Heath ;no deaths were reported and the outbreak seemed to he on the decline. Other slight cases of fever in the authority's district were mentioned, but they were not of a serious nature. The Inspector (Mr. Farrington) submitted his usual report. The business was of a routine character. CHRISTMAS TREE AT WIDNES.—The scholars of Milton Congregational Sunday school, Widnes, on Tuesday even- ing held a Christmas Tree, sale of work, and concert, is the Matins Temperance Hall. Mr. Eystace Carey opened the proceedings at five o'clock, when there was a fair attendance. The Rev. R. G. Hughes, the Rev. R. Yeatman, and Mr. Reay were amongst those present. The tree, on which were the usual miscellaneous articles, was presided over by the Messrs. Hirst, Doming, Phillips, and Chapman. Mrs Lewis and the Misses Travis, Thomas, and Warne presided over the workstall, and the Misses Williams and Knight over the refreshment stall. A short programme of vocal and instru- mental music, including a selection by handbell ringers, and an amusing exhibition and entertainment was gone through daring the evening, under the presidency of Mr. R. Yeat- man. Miss Travis ably officiated as accompanist. FATALITY TO A. WIDNES WOREMAN.—Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Adelphi Hotel, Warrington-road, Widnes, touching the death of William Barley, aged 31, formerly employed at the works of the Tharsis Copper Company, and living up to the time of his death at 33, Walmsley-street. Mr. C. El. Lewin, solicitor, appeared on behalf of the company, who were also represented by Mr. W. S. Pritchard, manager. It appeared that on the 14th instant one of the trucks on the high level tramway, 20 feet above the ground, left the metals. Bailey was attempting to replace the truck, when he slipped, and fell to the ground, sustaining a fracture of the skull and other injuries. A band rail ran along the tramway at a height of three feet, and a workman named William Pierce, of Farrant-street, did not consider there was any danger in working on the tramway. snow was falling at the time of the accident.—The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death." and suggested that another rail should be placed alongside the tramway in order to afford the workmen greater protection. POPULAR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Despite the exceed- ingly unfavourable weather, an audience of good propor- tions assembled in the Public .Hall on Saturday evening on the occasion of the fourth concert of the series promoted by the Mill Brow Military Band. The entertainment was one of the best that has been provided, and was thoroughly en- joyed by these present. The chief vocalist was Mr. George Barton, the well-known tenor, and be received a hearty wel- come from his numerous admirers. He was in capital voice, and sang with all his old fire and skill "The Bay of Biscay," "Draw the sword, Scotland." and "The anchors , weighed." He was heartily recalled after each effort. Miss Simkin, a contralto of local repute, contributed 'Uncle John" and "The song for me" in good style, and she was encored. Mr. Wilson Blackledge succeeded in highly diverting the audience by his humotr.ous songs and sketches, which were given with good effect. Mr. A. E. Pierpoint gave a performance on the clarionet, in which he showed much skill and no little training, and he was cordi- ally applauded. As usual, the band played several admir- able selections, under the conductorship of Mr. Oathwaite, and their execution gave much pleasure to an appreciative company. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—OD Tuesday afternoon the usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dut- ton Workhouse, Lieut.-Colonel Ashton presiding. There were also present Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Knowles, Aaron, Parr, W. Whitlow, Lowe, Brandreth, Hadfield, Farrell, Taylor, Camplein, Hamilton, J. Whitlow, Hewitt, Jackson;Forster, Percival, Pickering, Baguley, Speakman. Smith, Wallington, Moun- field, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk) , —The Board went into committee to consider the amount of superannuation of the late master and matron of the Work- house, Mr. and Mrs. Jones, and afterwards it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Campkin, seconded by Mr. Parr, that the superannuation be fixed at £5O for the master and 1-30 for the matron, to commence from the time of his leaving the service of the Board.—On the proposition of Mr. Camp. kin, seconded by Mr. Speakman, it was resolved that the salary to the present master and mistress, Mr. and Mrs. Connor, be increased by £2O a year, in consequence of an intimation from the Local Government Board that the amount to be repaid to the Guardians for the maintenance of the children of the master and matron was more than the I Guardians had understood to be the case.—Mr. Brandreth said that it had been decided to give the inmates of the Workhouse a treat at Christmas, and a suggestion had been made that tobacco should be provided for them. The law did not allow that the cost of that should come ou4 of the rates, and he proposed that a collection should be made at that meeting to raise the money required.—Mr. Lowe: I think the smokers should do that. (Laughter.)—The Deputy Clerk said that he had usually made a collection for oranges fcr the children, and it was agreed to make one to purchase both tobacco and oranges.—Mr. Brandreth caused some amusement by going round with the hat, amidst cries of "Look in his hat when he's finished," "Look after the lining," "Do you charge commission?" and "He's some wax on his fingers, maybe." The collection realised £1 4s 61—This was the principal bush:eve , Sneer. WE KNOW THEM AGAIN." This book containing be utiful Autotype Phoiogranhs of the late Bishon of Man- chest:ir. Mr. John E • wks, !LP.. and other faithful Christlans , may now be tbtained through any booksellers.—Advt.

Again, the sluggish WIDE PUBLICITY AT A CHEAP RATE. animal is said to be sulky, dangerous, and vindictive; Advertisement' received at any of the District Offices, or may and he again it is assumed that the proper remedial sent to the Chief Offices. Warrington. Stamps recely'd for measures are beating and harsh treatment. By such MOunt4r under means the animal of lively temperament is driven to viciousness, and the sluggish temperament is converted into obstinacy. Their descendants, carrying with them the bad name, are subjected to similar treatment, and thus they are credited with hereditary vice. The more young animals are brought into kindly asso- ciation with man, the more valuable will they be to their owners. In this association kindness and gentleness should be the predominating attributes, mixed with a firmness which should never degenerate into brutality. All animals are keenly alive to kindness, and their grati- tude exceeds the human feeling. They are not less equally sensitive of harsh treatment, arid, after many years of close personal observation, and inquiry, the writer has no hesitation in stating that when an animal attacks a human being who has been in association with it, the at- tack is in answer to brutal treatment that the animal has at some time received from the genus man. In proof of this, would your space permit, we could cite many interesting and well-authenticated cases. However, for the purposes of this article, two will suffice. The owner of a bull was under the impression that bulls required to be kept in subjection, and was in the habit of severely beating it whenever the animal showed the least signs of spirit. The attendants warned the master that the animal would do him a mischief if ever the opportunity occurred. He laughed at the caution, and said the bull knew that he was its master. One day the bull was being led out to water in charge of two men; the master entered the yard; scattering the two men like ninepins, the animal made for his owner, knocked him down, and, despite the efforts of the two men, so gored him that he was left a cripple for life. In the struggle the bull never attempted to injure the two attendants. We had a two-year old bull, full of spirit, but not difficult of control, and he had never shown evidence of vice. One day a neighbour remarked that he needed correc- tion, and brought his walkine, stick on the animal several times with force. The 'bull never forgot him, and the sound of his voice in the yard was sufficient to throw the animal into a state of violent excitement, making the most frantic efforts to tear out his head stake. The man who thrashed him took care never to enter the yard when the bull was being led out. Whilst treating animals with gentleness and kindness, one thing should never be lost sight of, and that is to display sufficient firmness to convince them that the man is the master. When necessary to restrain the exuberance of spirits in young animals, a whip is the best corrective, one smart stroke of which will be fouud sufficient. If you continue the chastisement it degenerates into bru- tality, and the object of the correction is not only lost, but you spoil the animal. If you wish for the maximum of profit from each and every animal of the farm, the above system of • treatment is necessary. It applies equally to horses, cows, bulls, dogs, sheep, and even pigs, for a fierce farrow sow can be won over to gentle- ness by constant human association and rubbing. It is not only necessary that the owner should practice this treatment, but he must take pains to ensure, and the result will amply repay him, that it is practised in its entirety by everyone in his employ. A man or boy who is cruel to animals, or afraid of them., should not be allowed to remain on a farm, for in either case he will effect mischief.

The CLBnIE. reported that in 14 new cases and 46 old cases school fees had been allowed by the School Fees Corn- inittw3.—On the motion ot Mr. BLACEHURST, seconded by Mr. BROWN, the minutes of this committee were adopted.

THE MURDER AT RAINHILL ASIVOM. The Clerk having read a communication as to the cost of maintenance of certain peeper lunatics in asylums, Mr. BreactcrtunsT referred to the recent murder of a lunatic by a fellow inmate in Rainitill Asylum, the murdered man'a name being Newton, who was formerly a flatholic priest in Warrington, and he (Mr. Blackliurst) asked whether or not Newton's maintenance had been paid for out of the rates of the Union.—The CLERK said that when Newton became lunatic a question arose as to his maintenance, and he (the clerk) found on inquiry into the matters of deceased father's estate that there was no possibility of getting anything from that direction. Iu the Roman Catholic Church, how- ever, when a man was ordained a priest he became the child of the bishop, and he (the clerk) put himself in communica- tion with the Bishop of Nottingham on the subject, and claimed that as he was the father of Newton —Mr. VorelY at this point interposed, and asked if it were necessary to go into all these details. He did not see any great necessity for it, the simple question having been asked as to whether Newton had been maintained at the cost of the Unien—and he thought an answer " Yes." or "No," to that would be sufficiont.—The CLERZ said if he had to answer it in that way he would say "No," and "Yes."—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the clerk was only making an explanation in answer to a request of a guardian.—Mr. Hartarsorr felt sure that the clerk did not wish to hurt the susceptibilities of any one, and suggested that the matter be allowed to drop where it was.—Mr. BROWN differed from Mr. HARRISON, am'. was of opinion that if the deceased had been chargeable to the rates it ought to be explained how it came to be so.—Mr. RATCLIFFE was of opinion that they had a perfect right to know all about the matter. It was something that would be useful to the members of the Board hereafter, and he did not think it should affect any one's, religious feelings.—Mr. GREENING Bahl be believed the deceased was a pauper lunatic for a certain letireth of time.—The CLERK said he would simply answer the goes-. tion that had been put to him "Yes." and "No,'.' but he hoped no one would hereafter get up and say he had given an answer which conveyed al meaning to their mind. , (Hear, hear.)—The matter then dropped.—lt was afterwards mentioned that part of the maintenance of deceased had been paid for by the Bishop.

On the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. GREEN- Iwo, Dr. Jack was formally appointed medical officer of No. 1 medical district, it being mentioned that he had now removed into the district.
THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S CASE.--FULL STlagelleST 13-X
THZ CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN said the members would see from the air ,- altar that had been sent to them a notice that the " Babied ot the workhouse master's resignation will be considered and resolutions passed thereon." It had occurred to him, seeing the great interest taken and very properly/taken by the members of that Board and others in the question at issue between the Local Government Board and Mr. Mac. key, and seelmg. teo, that the matter was being repeatedly discussed at their meetings, he thcught it might lae cif ad- vantage if he wrote down and read to them a brief *aternent of the simple actual facts that healed up to and4constituted the Present situation. In doing so he would premise that while he had taken every care to ascertain the facts, he bald himself open to conviction if any of his data we ques- tioned. In January, 1885, it appeared that some plumbing work was required at the workhouse, and an order atts given • to Mr. Hedgcock to carry it out. Whendone the invoice at. tached to the order should have been filed up, and the charges made for time and materia4, if reasonable, Entered in the roaster's day-book, to be paid with other accounts at the end of the quarter. In the following April, all accounts entered in the master's day-book to Lady Day were paid, and in July all accounts for goods or work doae daring the quarter ending at midsummer were paid, but in the secrind week of July Mr.. Hedgcock's bill was entered is the master's day-book and presented to the Board. The invoice represented work to hare been dene in Jane, it was initialled, examined, and uttered by the master, and signed as correct by the clerk, and returned with other invoices to the master. In Odober the accounts to Michaelmas were duly paid and entered, a bill being made out in the usual form in favour of Mr. Hedgcock. This bill, agreeing with the entry inile dew. book, was allowed by the House Committee and Paid by tie Board. They now came to 1886. In January the audit of the accounts for the half-year ending Michaelmas, 1885, took place, and on the Tuesday the auditor discovered that ithere was an erasure and alteration in Mr. Hedgcooles in. voice. He sent for the porter's book and found out that the work charged for in the bill bad been done in the previous January. EER LITTLE WORLD. .7% "My little world is very small, . k Scarce worth your notice, sir, at all," The mother said. "My good, kind husband, as you see, 3 And those three children at my knee, '`,* Who look to us so trustingly For daily bread.
f

"For their sweet sakes, who love me so, I keep the fire light in a glow , In our dear home. - That, though the tempests roar outside, And fiercely threaten far:and wide. The cheery blaze may serve toireuide • . „ Dear feet that roam. "And as the merry kettle boils •;,,- - 4:1/ We welcome him who daily toils For us each day. Of true love kisses full a score He gets, I'm certain, if not more, .-----i- When fond ones meet him at the door, ) ~........", At twilight grey. ._ . A "One gets his slippers for his feet - . 4 Another leads him to his seat— The big arm chair— . ~._ And while the children round him sing, And make the dear old rafters ring, ' One little daughter crowns him king, -...; With blossoms fair. .

"Ah, sir, we are not rich Or great, The owners of a vast estate," The mother said; "But we have better far than gold, ..4E' Contentment, and a little fold As full of love as it can hold, **" With daily bread." Mns. M. A. KIDDIII2.

I have been afflicted for about fourteen years with an obstinate skin disease called by some doctors eczema, and ' others, psoriasis. My body and hands were covered with Itching scabs, and during this time I have constantly used gloves. From South America; where I was for many years established. I have travelled through Spain, Portu- gal and France. where I have consulted several physicians of acknowleoged celebrity, tried hundreds of remedies, not one having the least effect. My friends here and else- where know that I have been a great sofferee. and that my condition at times has been such as to make me despair of ever being able to find a cure. or even a relief to my sick- ness. Last summer I again went to Paris, directly to the tit. Louis Hospital, but instead of finding any cure I was at death's dsor. AZARMING RAILWAY ACUIVENTS. An afarming raZway ?;ccident occurred ere Tuts-• day morning, on the London and North-Westerni ,Railway, outside the London-road Station, , Manchester. A slew train, for Stockport VMS des— patchedafe-w minctes after half-past nine, but; was 4 stopped at the distrAce signal, as the line was not clear, and the block systerm commences at thief, point. The station officials were not aware that the train had been stopped, and about ten minutes, afterwards a Birmingham express was sent out. A, dense fog prevailed at the time, and the driver be- ing unable to see the signals ran into the rear of the Stockport train. Fortunately he was proceeding cautiously or the result would have been most dis-- astrons. As it was the goods Tan of the Stockport train was smashed, and) several other carriages, were da-maged. Two passengers, in the Birming-- ham train were injured, and were taken to the In- - firmary,- whilst several psssengemin the Stockport train were slid:len, and the guard' was also slightly - injured.

-While a Great Northern passenger train from Woolwich•was standing at, a platform of Spa-road Station cf the South-Eastern Railway, on Tuesday morning, ithwas run into by a, train of empty wag- gons going to the Bricklayers' Arms Station. The brake of the former was smashed, and the guard SO much injured that he had to be taken to the hoe- pital. Several passengers alsoicomplained of having been severelY, shaken. TralE6 was much delayed, not only by the accident, but by fog. On Tuesday morning, the second of the night Scotch exuressses-from Euston came' into collision at Carlisle, with a Midland engine, throwing the latter off the rails. Both engines were much dam- aged, but no one was hurt, although the steps of the carriages cf the express were stripped off. The cause of the accident was the frost interfering with the action of thevacnum brake, the express rim- fling forward some-distance throagh the station and coming into collisien with the Midland engine on the north side.

WARRINGTON STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY'. On Monday evening, the first appropriation meet- ing in connection with this Society was held in • Cairo-street School. - In the absence of the ex.-Mayor (Alderman Harrison; through indisposition, Alder- man J. Davies was elected to preside. There were also present Messrs. N. Legge, T. Burton;.o. Lea, W. Crampton, D. Summers, J. Griffith, J. E. Wright, Titchett, &c. There was a good attendance,—ln a few prefatory remarks, the CHAIRMAN"' said he felt that the introduction of the Starr-Bowkett Build- ing Society into Warrington must prove of good to the inhabitants, and he should have said the same of any other building society. He was glad to see that in some towns Saarr-Bowkett Building Socie- ties had lad great success, while in other towns they had had moderate success. It was very good for working'men to commence saving;. for it was a solace to them and their families whenthey knew they had something to fall back upon. (Hear, • hear.) It was likewise good for the community, I for if the majority of -their countrymen acquired I saving habits he believed that they should •I destroy that socialistic evil which seemed to be growing in this country. They would therefore be I doing good by saving people from the, pauperism that seemed to be attached to socialistic notions. .1 (Hear, hear.) He then advised the members not to build, but to purchase property newly built if it could be done. From the experience he•had had in I connection with other societies, he had found that those men who bought property ready built seemed to do better than those who built it. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, he said he was pleased to see the directors they had elected. He had looked over their names, and to his mind they seemed to be all men upon whom they ,could depend, always bear- ing in mind that the directors were the servants of the members. and that i they could get better men they should elect them. (Applause.)—Mia.CoLLlNGs, of Bolton, then gave an address—similar to the one we reported on the formation of the society— explanatory of the aims and objects, and methods of working Of the Starr-Bowkett Building Socie- ties. He mentioned that the Warrington Society had now about 170 members, holding something like 380 or 390 shares, and thishe could tell them, con- sidering the short time the society had been estab- lished, was above the average. (Applause.)—At the conclusion of the address, several persons gave in their names as members. In answer t 3 a question as to whether a member of the society who had removed from Warrington could purchase property in the town into which heehad moved, Mr. Collings answered in the affirmative, and also explained the methods, adopted in such a case, and the mode in which the payments were made by a member who had removed from the town in which the society was established.—Afterwards the first appropria- tion was made, Alderman Davies, in accordance with the rules, vacating the chair, and a member, Mr. Jukes, being elected to take his place. Messrs. Horton and Whitehouse were also elected to act as scrutineers of the ballot. The result of the ballot was the drawing of 49; which proved to be the registered number of Mr. T. Egerton, joiner, Robson- street, Warrington, who . was declared to be en- titled to the use of £2OO free of interest. The meeting was afterwards brought to a close by votes I of thanks to Alderman Davies and others who had conducted the business of the meeting.

SALYATIOK ARMY SCANDAL. AT ST. HELENS. ALLEGED ELOPEMENT. John Sims, a young man, applied to the magis- trates, Alderman Harrison and Mr. B. Biram, at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday test, for a warrant for the ; apprehension of his wife, Alice Sims. The applicant is a t glasstnaker at Messrs. Pilkington's works, and lived in Lyon-street with his wife, Alic;e, and their one child. Another young man engaged in the SitTle trade, also mar- ried, and living in the same etreet, is said to have disap- peared along with Mrs. Sims. Mrs. Sims disappeared on ; Saturday night, and her husband suspected that his wife 1 had taken money, clothing, valuables, ,be. These included a silver lever watch, breast pin, pair of sleeve links, locket, chain, and gold ring, altogether valued at £7 17s. Sims was not able to give satlefactery answers to the questions , put to him by the magistrates and the clerk (Mr. Davison) as to who witnessed Mrs. Sims take the articles from the house. He said the things were missing, his wife was missing, aed Grey was- missing, and he had no doubt but that they had the articles. Eventually the magistrates.. told him to get further particulars and make another appli- cation. At the Police Court, on Tuesday, before the Mayor (Col. Gamble) and Lieut.-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, the young man John Sims, of Lyon-street. again appeared, and made a further application of a similar nature. He said he wanted a warrant for the apprehension of his wife. On Saturday night he was at work at Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks, and about eight o'clock his wife brought him his supper. . At ten o'clock he went home, and found that his wife had gone. He went upstairs and found that her clothes : were gone; also a silver lever watch, gold breast- pin, silver links, silver locket, chain, and gold ring, which his wife had purchased with his money.— The Assistant Clerk (Mr. Davidson) : Have you made any further inquiries since Monday ? Sims: I went to Liver- pool to a shop where she bad purchased a sealskin jacket for 12 guineas, but I had told the man who brought it that he must take it baek, and he did so. On inquiry I found that Grey had been to the shop on Saturday night, bought the jacket, and said he was in a hurry to catch the 7-40 train to St. Helena—The Clerk: Did you ascertain anything about them going away together P—Sims: I heard nothing until I got home. My little girl showed me a needle, and said that was what my wife was stitching up the things with, and that she came downstairs with her hest bat on. I have a young woman who saw a cab at the door, but she dicta% see anyone get into it.—Colonel Pilkington: The man is missing, I suppose P—The Clerk: Yes. But the law says that a woman cannot steal from her husband while she lives. with him: The question is—was she going away with this man, and taking her husband's things. with her Sims : I was Old the woman came in for them, and that Grey stopped outside.—Colonel Pilkington: It seems to me that it is a case that should come before the magistrates. If the case is to he fully proved before a warrant is granted, what is the use of coming again into court? The man and woman and things have disappeared. It seems to me a great mistake that the warrant was not gran- ted on Monday. The Clerk There was no eyideece to justify a warrant being granted. Sims : There are evon cups and saucers missinbut I don't know exactly yet what is gone.—Colonel Pilkington: There is not the shadow of a doubt that this fellow has gone with the woman.—Sims : It is three weeks since she went and drew 20() out of the bank, money' that was in her name And in mine jointly. One could draw it as well as the other.— After some further discussion between the magistrates and the clerk, Sims said he was prepared to swear that his wife had taken the things away.—The Clerk: Very well; then I suppose a warrant will be grastel,--Colonel Pilkington And what about the man ?,--The Clerk : J!suppose she took the things and then jorted the man —Sims, in reply to the magistrates, said he was married eight years since at Eccleston Church.—A warrant for the appreheitaion of Mrs. Sims was granted. It is stated . that George Grey was "an ex-sergeant " in, the local contingent of the Salvation Army, and that Sims, the applicant, held the same rank. This brought the families. , together very frequently. Mrs. Sims left her husband and, one little girl. It is stated that Grey had seen beard to nip at work that he would go to Australia, and would not work in England again. The affair hal Car.led great ezriitzateg% and gossip in the town,

A good action is never forgotten—by an attorney. 'im VOICES OF THE Ntour.—Those blessed babies. The man who was "filled with emotion" hadn't room for his dinner. He that would be sure to have his business well done, must either do it himself, or see to the doh4g of it. It was a maxim with Cesar, that we ought to reckon 'We have done nothing, so long as anything remains to be

done. Men can never quite grasp one another's hands. There- fore, when he wants any intimate help, any genuine heart- sustenance, he must look to woman. We may hate men's vices, without any ill-will to their persons; but we cannot help despising those that have no kind of virtue to recommend them. Smith "I notice that milkmen, as a rule, wear very heavy shoes." Brown: "Because, you know, it would be rather suggestive if they wore pumps." SO DID HE.—An agent for the sale of rugs had rung the door bell of a house on Montcalm-street several times, when a man came to the door with a squalling baby under his arm and asked what he wanted. "I'd like to see the lady of the house!" was the reply. "And so would I! She ran away three days ago, and I'd like to see her long enough to give her a piece of my mind &out leaving this howling kid behind her!" A member of Parliament, well known for his ready and unfailing humour, had lately to undergo a serious operation in the leg. It was at one time feared that am- putation would be necessary. Just as the operation was about to begin the honourable member quietly remarked to the surgeon, "Remember that if you cut off my leg I can't stand for the borough any more." "But," he added, after a pause, as if for consideration, "after all, I.shall be able to stump the country." WISE USE OF DISAPPOINT3IENT.—You may be almost confident that those who in mature life are the habitually cheerful and even buoyant are they who have known most of trial or have suffered most of wrong. Such rare sweetness have I sometimes seen among the former slaves of this land as well as among the poorest peasantry of other shores. I have seen it too where few knew the secret sorrow of the life.—To lose the wise use of such disappointment and trial as God permits in our lives is one of the greatest possible losses. "Will you pay me this bill?" said a tailor in Regent- street, to a genuine masher who owed him a pretty long bill. "Do you owe anybody anything. sir ?" asked the youth. "No, sir," said the tailor. "Then you can afford to wait," and off he walked. A day or two afterwards the tailor called again. The masher was not at his wits' end yet, so, turning tohis creditor, he says: "Are you in debt to anybody ?" "Yes, sir," said the tailor. "Then, why don't you pay?" "I've not got the money." "That's just my case, sir. I am glad to see you can - appreciate my condition; give us your hand!" AN ANCIENT RECEIPT FOR MAKING THUIsIDE'R.—In the middle ages anybody at all distinguished by knowledge of science was credited with the art of flying, and indeed in many cases did not scruple to claim it. Albertus Magnus was one of these, but refused to give particulars to the world at large. He tells us, however, how to make thunder. Says he :—" Take one pound of sulphur, two pounds of willow carbon, and six pounds of rock salt, ground very fine in a marble mortar; place where you please in a covering made of flying papyrus to produce thunder. The covering, in cider to ascend and float away, should be long, graceful, and well filled with this powder, but to produce thunder the covering should be short and thick and half full." JUDGE KEOGH AND TIM WITNESS.—Judge Keogh, who, by the way, was hated of all men in Ireland, was one day adjudicating in a case, the point of which had re- ference to a document that the defence endeavoured to show had been signed when the prosecutor was drunk. Under cross-examination the following dialogue took place in court. The defending barrister: "Now, sir, will you tell his Lordship what you had to drink on that occasion before you signed the document?" "Indeed, your honour," said the witness, "I don't think a gentle- man need say what he had to drink for dinner." "I think you are bound to answer the question," said Judge Keogh, solemnly. "Did you take sherry, sir?" de- manded the barrister. "Well, yes, I had a couple of glasses of sherry." "'And did you take claret and cham- pagne?" "No; I don't drink either," was the answer. "Now, sir, after dinner did you have some whisky?" "Certainly, I had some whisky." "Now, on your oath, did you have three glasses of whisky ? " "I must appeal to your Lordship. Am I bound to answer the question ? " "Yes," answered Keogh, with a laugh; "I think you are." "Very well," replied the witness. "I had three glasses of whiskey." "Now, sir, will you :say it was not five?" "Again I appeal to your Lord- ship," said the witness; and, meeting with no answer, said: "Well, yes," it was five." "Will you swear, sir, it was not ten ? " A mute glance of appeal towards the bench, and then came the answer: I will not swear." "Upon your oath, was it not fifteen?" "Well, yes; it was fifteen." "Now then, sir, I ask you was it not twenty?" "No, sir; it was not twenty." "Oh, oh," said the barrister. "Here is a gentleman who drinks two glasses of sherry at dinner, and admits having had fifteen tumblers of whiskey, and yet is able to remember that he did not take twenty. Now, sir, how do you recollect it was not twenty?" "Why, then, I'll tell you," and, turning to the Judge, the wit- nees said "You will remember, your honour, we were at dinner together, and afterwards, coming downstairs, I said to you have had eighteen tumblers of whisky and you said Then I have beaten you, for I have had twenty 1" There were roars of laughter in court, in which Keogh joined, for he had anticipated the de- nouement. ANIMAIS FOND OF FERFTTME.—Within the last year, I have had the opportunity of noting the ways of the various wild beasts which inhabit G. Sanger's mena- gerie at Margate. The keeper studies the idiosyncracies of each animal with the closest attention, and never em- ploys violence in their treatment. Of course, some animals are more susceptible to kindness than others, just as is the case among human beings. A short cut to the heart of any of the large felidee is to be found inlavender water, a fact which I discovered by accident. The late Mrs. Lee, whose leopard " Sai " was so interesting an in- mate of her household, trained the animal almost only by taking advantage of its love for this perfume. So, wanting to be on good terms with the leopard "Old Maa," I took some lavender-water with me. Before giving it to the leopard, I thought I would try the effect an " Bessy," a fine tigress, who has for some time been very „aracious in her conduct towards me. I poured a few drops of the perfume on a small piece of brown paper and held it to her. She first gave a, prolonged sniff, and then scraped the paper out of my hand, and laid it on the floor of the cage. First, she sniffed at it repeatedly. raising her nose high in the air after every sniff. Then stie tore it into little pieces, which she strewed over the tear. Then she rolled over and over on the perfumed fragments, giving a series of muffled yelps of delight, and then began leaping all over the cage, springing up until her head struck against the roof,turning over in the air, and coming down on the boarded floor with a mighty thump, as might be expected from an animal weighing more than 300 pounds. Next, I tried the effect on the leolaard "Old Man," who occupied the neighbouring cage, and found that he was even more affected than the tigress, slobbering over the perfume until the floor of the cage was quite wet, and rolling over and over, ex- actly as his neighbour had done. Meantime "Erispress," who occupied a cage on the opposite side of the banding, had scented the lavender-water from a distance, and was loudly expressing her opinion that she had been shame- fully neglected. So I gave her a liberal dose of the per- fume, and she, being only a young thing, and unaccus- tomed to self-control, straightway proceeded to go mad over it. After she had exhausted the last particle of per- fume, I happened to pass in front of the cage. With a loud roar and outstretched arms, she flew at the bars, Vlaway the flat folding bars at the lloor of the cage, t her arms out as far as the elbows, and looked ex- actly as if she meant to eat up evetyone in the building. litiare was a shriek of alarm on the part of a number of viertors, accompanied by a rush f• the door. But there was no harm m the animal. SA only wanted another svpply of the unaccustomed luxury, took it quite gently alad reeerrinaenced her antics. WIWI'. ms KOMPO ?
