ANTHRAX IN CATTLE.—In a recent issue of the Lancet is a very interesting history of an outbreak of anthrax in cattle, and wtierewith nine men were infected. It is one of the specimens of the blundering of our too much law system that anthrax was not placed under the Con- tagious Diseases (Cattle) Act long ago, and not left until agitation had to be got in order to bring the matter be- fore the authorities. DOCKING HORSES TAILS.—The "Medical and Profes- sional Review" draws attention to the question of dock- ing horses's tails. It will be remembered that a few weeks ago a case was heard at the Chorley Police-court, in which a man was fined for performing the operation, and this decision has excited some controversy. The journal named says :—" There is still much difference of opinion, whether amputating horses' tails is illegal or not. It seems a pity that some definite decision cannot be arrived at by the members of the profession with respect to it. It has been suggested to petition the President of the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons to allow the college solicitor to look up this matter with a view to publishing the particulars, requesting that gentleman to cite for the purpose any Act of Parliament or order bearing on the question, and to furnish a copy of the clause or clauses declaring the practice to be illegal. Veterinary surgeons will then be in a position to explain to their clients that refusal to comply with the requisi- tion is in obedience to the law. Probably at the present time the only individuals who refuse to operate are to be found amongst the veterinary profession, and these the very persons who could perform the task with the least degree of pain to the animal. At present there have been as many convictions for docking horses as there have been dismissals, so that until a judge's decision has been obtained, the subject will remain in dispute." THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—At the last meet- in.- of the Council of the Royal Agricultural Society, at which there were present ford Egerton of Tatton (in the chair), Earl Cathcart, Earl Spencer, Lord Moreton, Sir M. White-Ridley, Bart., M.P., Air. Foster, Mr. Jacob Wilson, and other gentlemen, Dr. Voelcker, the consult- ing chemist, presented a report, stating that a consider- able amount of analytical work has been done in the society's laboratory in connection with the experiments conducted by local societies. The report further stated that " Comp_ptition among seed crushers and manufac- turers of artificial manures, whilst cheapening the materials used on the farm, has not had an altogether beneficial effect as regards their purity or general reliability. More cases than previously have been brought under the notice of the Chemical Committee in which impure or inferior articles have been purchased as genuine, or at prices far above their intrinsic worth. Little or no improvement has taken place in the supply of decorticated cotton-cake, it being a matter of difficulty to get a cake the mechanical condition and chemical composition of which are really good. When on offer, a good cake is snapped up almost immediately, and it is a great pity that more care is not exercised in the manu- facture of this valuable cake. The price has, however, fallen lower and lower, until there is often hardly any difference between the cost of decorticated and unde- corticated cake. He and there cakes with 13 per cent. or even 20 per cent. of oil have been met, but the generality rarely exceed 11 or 12 per cent."— An application by Mr. Arthur Gibbs to be appointed seedsman to the society, in succession to his late father, was refused, it being thought undesirable to invest any firm with the prestige of the society. The prizes for en- gines, Sze., at the next7show were decided upon. It was stated that prizes amounting to £5O had been offered by the Mayor of Newcastle for classes for aged shire stallions. It was decided to offer a prize of £25 for a one-man power cream separator, the price not to exceed £2O, and to be capable of dealing with 20 gallons of milk per hour.—Responding to a, vote of thanks at the general meeting which followed, Lord Egerton said allusions had been made to the existing depression, and it was suggested that this society should do something towards its removal. He thought that it was at present en- deavouring to show the British farmer how he could cultivate most economically. To demonstrate the effi- cient placing of good seeds and manures in the land, the quantity, Sze., could only be arrived at by a variety of experiments, and the Royal Agricultural Society had done their best to assist several of the local societies who were endeavouring to c irry out experiments with this object. LONDON CHRISTMAS CATTLE MARKET,—Following closely on the heels of the agricultural show at Islington came the usual annual animal market for the sale of fat stock for Christmas consumption. British beef still holds the lead, and it is to be hoped it will be a long time be- fore the sirloin grown on our pastures will have to suc- cumb to foreign competition, whether from Germany or across the Atlantic. In its main features the show did not differ very materially from previous exhibitions; excellent qualitia and condition are invariably looked for on these occasions, and seldom in vain. The show had the usual satisfactory ev,enness, and may be classed as a success. The Scotch exhibits were the prominent feature of the market. They were a goodly number, and their appearance left little to be desired. But there were at the same time some splendid Herefords, as well as Devons. The cress-bred was well represented, as it de- serves to be, seeing it is as profitable an animal as any in the market. Really inferior stock seems to be gradually disappearing. Breeding has now become a science, and it does not pay to produce coarse, heavy-boned stock. A maximum of flesh on a minimum of bone is the aim to attain which such considerable strides have of recent years been made. The continental graziers are now sending us a much more useful animal than they formerly did, and the character of the American receipts keeps up. It will not do therefore for our breeders to rest on their laurels or relax their efforts towards further improving their already excellent stock. The Irish beasts still show plenty of room for improvement. Very slow progress is made by the sister isle, notwithstanding her fine grazing facilities. BUTTER.—DOES IT PAY TO MAKE A GOOD ARTICLE ? "B." (Ulverston) writes: "Does it pay to make the best butter? At country markets, butter, whether good or bad, all sells at a price, or nearly so. There can be no doubt but that both controversialists are right from their different standpoints, and that both good and bad butter is made. The chief point to be considered is, does it pay to take pains, and make the best article? There are some makers who always command a ready market for their butter, and to whom the top price is paid, because the purchasers have customers who bespeak this par- ticular butter, and are content to pay a little money for it. Butter in the local markets is usually quoted, say, from is. 2d. to is. 3d. per lb. The price paid to farmers by shopkeepers and customers, by lodging-house keepers, &c., who do not purchase in the market, is thesmiddle figure, that is, is. 2kd per lb. Now, supposing, , for example, that 501 b. of butter per week is made at a farm. By making a good article, you sell it at an advance of d. per pound, or a profit of 2s. id. ttupposing even that you make a superfine butter, and you get an advance of id. per lb., or 4s. 2d. over the inferior article, does it pay? Well, you have the satisfaction of making a good marketable commodity; but if you are careless of your reputation as a butter-maker, if you leavethe milk I in, the 501 b. of butter is swollen to 601 b. Sixty pounds of poor butter at is. 2d.---£3 10s. for the inferior article; 551 b. of middling or good butter at is. 20.--£3 6s. skd.; 501 b. of superfine, or the best butter that can be made, at is. 3da-s=£3 2s. 6d. Where is the inducement to make the best butter, for, as I before remark, in a country market it all sells ? " •

There is no just action, no kind word, no obliging de- meanour, no charity, no hospitality, that springs from selfishness which shall not have its penalty, inasmuch as it corrupts the character; and there is no kindness, no forbearance, no generosity, no charity, that springs from disinterested benevolence which has not its remu- neration, for it makes men better, nobler, and purer. The wife who gets into the way of contradicting and " checking " her husband, of opposing him in small things and standing out in large—the husband who is sneering, contemptuous, tyrannical, fault-finding perhaps neither side knowing the whole extent of its folly, but just giving way to it as more easy than to tight and conquer it—these young people are doing their best to dig the grave of their married peace. An Irish landlord noted for his bulk of person was lying seriously ill. A number of persons called to in- quire after him, among them one of his tenants. The man was informed that he was being kept up by the oc- casional administration of teaspoonsful of brandy; he at once rejoined somewhat contemptuously, " Tayspoons, .is it? And what good would a tayspoon be.sthraying about in such a wilderness of a man?' _ Truths can never conflict, for truth is a unity, and, when an opinion that has once been held is forced to give way under the pressure of advancing thought, it is but the outer shell that once contained a truth and is no longer needed which drops away, while the everlasting truth remains with all who are wise enough to retain it. Thus, in the world of thought, sameness must be the accepted foundation on which changes must gradually be made if any solid advancement is to be attained. HOMINY AND How To Coox Ir.—Oatmeal porridge is good, but it is too heating for some constitutions, and it may be supplanted with advantage by hominy in the spring. This, if well made, is simply delicious, and in the States is enjoyed by old and young alike; but it must be well cooked. A good plan is to soak it all night—two ounces of hominy in half a pint of cold water. In the morning put it in a saucepan, and cook for an hour, stirring often, adding more water as it thickens until another half-pint has been added. Serve with sugar and cream, or good milk. Some prefer less water, and milk to make the quantity, in which case the hominy and water must be cooked thoroughly first, and the milk added just before serving. Lined saucepans or those of fire-proof china are the most suitable for mak- ing porridge; better still the double saucepans—then i burning is mpossible. ENGLISH DECORATIVE NEEDLE WORR.—II is difficult to discover by what means Anglo-Saxon England arrived a such perfection in needlework. Already in the seventh Century after Christ, as we find from the wonderfully minute description of the grave-clothes of St. Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne, embroidery seems to have been in a high state of cultivation, practised, no doubt, by the monks or nuns of the ancient monastries. when the body of the saint was disinterred in the twelfth century, we are told that not Only his body but his grave-clothes had been miraculously preserved, the gold all untar- nished; and the linen sheet which covered him and the relics Which had been buried with him was, it would ap- pear from the description of that same early form of lace which we find on Egyptian monuments. But there is so much difficult, in determining from written records when the womk o the loom is referred to and when that Of the needle, that a. wide field is left for rival theorists. Some time before the Norman Conquest, however, we find Anglo-Saxon women adepts in the finer kinds of embroidery. The wife of Edward the Confessor was "perfect mistress Of her needle." William of Poictiers, secretary to William the Conqueror, states that "the English women are eminently skilful with the needle and in weaving of gold." William himself, in fact, appeared at his coronation in a splendidly-embroidered robe of Anglo-Saxon workmanship, from which we may gather that the art existed in England from much earlier times, and did not come thither from Normandy.—" The Maga- zine of Art" for December' Vor rough,. red, or chapped skin there is nothing equal-to " Beetham's Glycerine 501 Cucumber." WIT AND HUMOUR. _ - A correspondent asks: "Is it wrong to cheat a law- yer ?" First cheat the lawyer and we will answer the conundrum. Some one says it is the hill which produces the echo. And here we have lived all these years thinking it was the holler. Smith: My wife wants a new dress every day in the year.—Jones: She must be awfully extravagant. Does she get it 2—Smith: No; that's the reason she is com- pelled to want it. INDEED.—" Why is a small boy like a woman ?" said a New Hartford man to his troublesome wife. No re- sponse. "Because he will mike a man grown," said the conundrumist. Speaking of a new riding habit, the Boston Herald thinks that it will not be generally worn by the girls until a great many girls wear it. That seems clear enough, yet it is a trifle confusing. Henry George says the time will come when no man will be allowed to own land which he does not use. From that it will be only a step to the time when no man will be allowed to own anything which anybody else wants. RIGHT WAY TO PIDDLE A CANOE.—Snappish uncle: "No George, I'll not help you with a solitary shilling. You must paddle your own canoe." Despairing nephew: "But what with, uncle?" Snappish uncle, immediately: "A skull—like I did." Jawkin : That was a rather sudden death of old Skin- flint's. What was the matter with him ?—Hawkin : Economy. The two undertakers are running each other, and funerals are away in in price. Old Skin- flint never missed a bargain n his life. THE PROBABLE REASON.—Mr. Winks: Well, well! The paper says a rich Kentucky farmer, blessed with a charming wife and children, committed suicide by I hanging himself in his dining-room. What could have possessed the man 2—Mrs. Winks: I suppose the dinner I wasn't ready, dear. Three burglars worked all night on a safe in an office in Fond Du Lac, and when they finally got it open they found six postal cards and five postage stamps to reward them. The only revenge they could take was to paste 1 the stamps on the wall and write on one of the cards: "A feller who keep a big sfe without anything in it is a bloke !" WHAT KIND OF WATER.—Man at the water cooler (pausing reflectively in the midst of a drink) : What Iduci. of water is this ?—Native (reassuringly) : That? That's well water.—Man at the water cooler: You are too sanguine, my friend. This water May be conva- lescent, but it is gross satire to call it well. A JUVENILE INFERENCE.—" Mother," said a littleitock- land girl, looking up from her book, "what does trans- Atlantic mean ?" Oh, across the Atlantic, of course. Don't bother me, you make me forget my count." "Does trans always mean across ?" "I suppose it does. If you don't stop bothering me with your questions you'll go to bed." "Then does transparent mean a cross parent?" Mrs. Gilflory : I think it's a shame 1 have to ride about in that old chaise when Mrs. Spreadeagle is always getting something new in the way of a vehicle. —Mr. G.: Why, my love, surely she hasn't a new equipage, has she ?—Mrs. G.: Of course she has! I heard her say at her party the other evening that her husband had given her a carte hlanche.—Mr. G.: It's one of those basket phretons, I fancy.

WIDNES SCITOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Boar 4 was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P. Present—Messrs. W. Bradshaw, H. W. Deacon, J. W. Wareing, F. Heyes, Rev.. George Bond, mad Gt. panby (clerl9. - DISTRICT EDUCATION, The minutes af the District Education ComtnitteG passed on the motion of Mr. H. W. Deacon, stated that there were 103 applications for the payment of fees, and they were re- commended to be paid in 89 cases. There were 215 per- sons summoned before the committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 31 were prosecuted, and 30 con- victed.

AN EXTREME PROPOSAL. The School Management recommended that three months notice be given to all the teachers to terminate their engage- ments with the Board. Mr. Bond proposed the adoption of the proposal, and ex- plained that it was passed at a .-neeting of the committee, at which Father Finegan and himself were only present. Some of the reasults of the teachers were not what they ought to have been, and they proposed to terminate the engagements of all the teachers so that the Board might have an oppor- tunity of exercising their discretion as regarded the termin- ation of some of the engagements. The Chairman suggested that the recommendation should be referred back. He did not think' Mr. Bond was thoroughly posted up in the matter, and be was sure that gentleman had brought forward no reasons to justify such a motion. Mr. Bond: I think it is rather strong myself. I was not a party to it. He added that he could not give any reasons to justify the step, because be was quite new in the matter. He was sorry Father Finegan could not be present. Mr. Heves said that he understood that Father Finegan considered it desirable that the terms upon which the pupil teachers at present were engaged should be reconsidered, and be saw no way of doing this except by terminating the engagemeUt Te Moved that the minute be referred back. Mr Bond sal€l he had no bat ttieteaA6n was as stated by Mr. Heyes. The Chairman pointed out that the present scale of sala- ries had only been in operation for two years, and had worked'very well, and he was not aware of any reasons why a new scale should be introduced. It would be extremely unfair to all the teachers before there was a new scale. Mr. Wareing said this mode appeared to have been adop- ted in order to pat pressure on the teachers. Mr. Bond : There was no such idea. It was simply to save the ratepayers' pockets. Mr. Deacon said he utterly objected to the principle. In the works of the town it was usual to give notice of a reduc- tion, and allow the men an opportunity of accepting or not. There was nothing in that recommendation about a reduc- tion, or about saving the ratepayers' money. It was simply giving the teachers notice without warning and was utterly unjust, and he would not for one moment agree to it. Mr. Bond said the recommendation did not mean that they should act upon it at all. They gave notice which the teachers could accept or not. The minute was referred back. THE GRANTS. It was reported that the average grants per child in Widnes Board schools in 1886 was 19s 21d, an increase of 3f on the previous year. At Sinam's Cross school the merit grant of " excellent " was obtained by the senior boys, the junior boys, and the infants. While "good" was obtained by the senior girls and the junior girls. The average grant was 194 lid, an increase of 56 over 1885. At Warrington. read school the senior boys earned the "excellent" merit grant, the senior girls and junior girls "good." and the junior boys "fair." The average grant was 17s 3icl, a de- crease of lid. At West Bank the " excellent " merit grant was obtained by the senior boys, the junior boys, and the junior girls, and the senior girls and the infants received "good." The average grant was 18s 30, an increase of lid on 1885. The total grants earned in the whole of the schools was £2,405 7s lid, with an average attendance of 2,505. In 1885 the total grant was £2,226 31 86, with an average attendance of 2,354. Of the 39 pupil teachers and candidates 12 passed well, 9 fairly, and 18 were marked in one or more subjects. In 1835 38 were examined, and four passed well, 22 fairly, and 12 were marked in one or more subjects. In the cookery classes 278 were examined, and there was a grant of £55 12. The Chairman stated that the cookery teacher received £BO a year, but the practical cost to the Board was £24 Be Ode Mr. Wareing said he did not know how the committee could have framed such a resolution as the one they had just been discusssing in the face of such results. , REPAIRS AND ALTERATIONS. On the recommendation of the Sites and Building Coma mittee, the tender of Messrs. Lea and Son was accepted for the repairs and cleaning of West Bank and Warrington-road schools, and the tender of Mr. J. Beach was accepted for the repairs and cleaning at Simms Cross school. FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended that accounts amounting to £715 lie 7d be paid, and reported that the re- ceipts for November amounted to £1,453 4s ld. They also recommended that six months' notice be given to Mr. Rock to terminate' the tenancy of the present board room and offices. Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the minutes, and re- marked that the new public offices would be ready for occu- pation in March. THE VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS AND THE RATES. IMPORTANT DISCUSSION. Mr. Bond proposed that the following petition be for- warded to the Royal Commission on the Education Acts "That voluntary schools supply a certain amount of accom- modation for children which saves the district a large sum in the erection of fresh buildings, and thinks it only fair that they should have their share of the rates levied for schools under Government inspection, as with their limited resources they are unable. to provide all the appliances which are required and which all School Board schools can command. Secondly, that schools amid a scattered popula- tion should be judged by a different standard as regards average attendance and consequent efficiency than those around which a large population is concentrated. Thirdly, that all elementary schools should be exempt from all rates and taxes." Mr. Bond said ho thought it was his duty to propose this petition in accordance with what he said before he became a member of the Board. He argued that as the denomina- tional schools *ere a great help to the ratepayers, it Wa3 only fair that as the rates were levied on the whole of the population—on those who supportod the voluntary schools —that these schools should have a fair share of the rates. Besides, the denominational schools had been utterly starved out by the Education Act, and he would give them an in- stance in his own school at Farnvrorth. Mr. Peter Longton had given them a piece of land adjoining the school for a playground, and they had not the means to fence. it round. They could e.rnply keep the school afloat. They did not aek for any great amount from the rates, and did not ask for anV of the expenses of management. He had frequeutly to ad-
MINIIIMM•••••I
f"

vance a large sum of money to support his schools' and other persons no doubt had to do the lame. He alluded to the long distances children had to walk to attend Farnvrorth School, and he wrote a letter which was read before the Royal Commiesion, asking that there should be some differ- ence made in the standard with which these schools were judged from others. The last paragraph in the petition was Father Finegan's suggestion—that voluntary schools should be exempt from rates and taxes. The payment of these charges did not matter much to the Board schools, because they could dip their hands into the pockets of the ratepayers. but it was of great importance to the voluntary schools. They had enly the Government grant, the school pence, and a few—very few—subscriptions to depend upon, and the more the School Board rate the fewer subscrip- tions they got. Mr. Heyes seconded the motion, and expressed his con- currence with Mr. Bond's remarks. It seemed to him that the Department in making thp codes did everything they could to starve out voluntary schools, and he thought to levy rates and taxes upon them was a most unjust proceed- ing. He did not suppose that Government would agree to .contributo out of local rates to support voluntary schools unless they had some hand in the menagement—(ar. Ware- ing : Not likely)—but till be thought that something might be done to relieve the difficulties of the managers of voluntary schools, and he thought the petition was calcu- lated to do good. Mr. Deacon was sorry to have to oppose this motion with the exception of the third paragraph, to which he had no objection. It was not his wish to oppose voluntary schools in any way, but he believed that the result of the working of the Education Act of 1870 had been very favourable to those schools. If, as Mr. Bond said, voluntary schools were utterly starved out, supposing there were 8,281 voluntary schools in 1870, which was a matter of fact, the result one would naturally expect was that they would be fewer in number. On the contrary, in 1885 there were 14,600 vol- untary schools, so that by this exceedingly starving out Act those schools had increased by 6,319. In the same year there were 4,295 Board schools so that the voluntary schools bad increased much more rapidly than the Board Schools had been established. In voluntary schools in 1870 there were in average attendance 1,152,389 children and in 1885 that number had rieen to 2,183,870. an increase of 1,130,000. In 1885 the children in average attendance at Board schools numbered 1,187,455, so that there was ac- tually an increase in the attendance of voluntary schools equal fo the whole average attendance in the Board schools. In the face et these figures the allegation of "starving out " could Lot be maintained. 31r, 13ond did not Eay how rettiCh he wanted from the rates, nor how ha proposed that the money should be spent, but it would certainly mean a great increase on the ratee,asnd they received a great deal hotel the public puree. In 1870 the dovernment grant to voluntary schools was .£502,611, and in 1883 it was £1,822.801, an increase of mote than three times. The voluntary subscriptions in 1870 amounted to £418,839, while in 1885 they had increased to £755.936. The school fees dur- ing the same period had increased from £502,023 to .11,228,261, more than double. These figures made it very hard indeed to maintain that the Government or the people, or anybody else, wished. or had succeeded, in starving out the voluntary schools. The amount already paid from the public purse was simply enormous, being over a million and three quarters, and, as Mr. Heyes wisely said, they could not expect money to be paid from the rates without some practical representation of the ratepayers, and in the volun- tary schools the ratepayers are not represented. With regard to scattered 'populations and the average attendance, he sympathised with Mr. Bond, but did not agree with him in the way he would remedy it. He pointed out that under article 111 in the Code provision was made for an extra grant in such case. He should be extremely loth to lower either the efficiency or the average attendance, and he would suggest that section 111 should be amended. While quite willing to accept paragraph 3, he could not support the me- morial as it stood. The Chairman said there was no doubt the figures quoted by Mr. Deacon proved that voluntary schools had not suf- fered under the operations of the Education Act. The in- tention Of the Act was to support voluntary schools, it had been so administered, and the tesult had proved its effi- ciency. He should like to ask Mr. Bond whether he was quite sure he would like that petition passed. He very much doubted if ke did. They could not conceive it pos- sible that a lump sum would be paid from the rates to Mr. Bond. or Father Finegan, and that they should spend it as they liked. There was a very large class of their fellow- townsmen, and unfortunately they had no representatiye at that Board that day, who were strongly of opinion that what they taught at the church was error, and that what the Roman Catholics taught was error, and they would cer- tainly be up in arms and justly so, if their money_ was to be taken to teach what might be erroneous views. They W6td!.fi never get the House of Commons to pass such a law. At that Board the public money wag 'spent openly by properly elected representatives, and he did not think the denominational schools were prepared to allow the public to see how they Spent every half-penny of their money. Then if they had public money and public management they would cease to have control over their own schools—(hear, hear,)—and he (Mr. Bond) would not be absolute master, as he was now. The chairman also argued that aid from the rates would end in the extinction of the zeal of those connected with the schools and the voluntary subscriptions would cease; it would re-act, he believed, on the various churches, and ha thought to carry out the proposal contained in the first paragraph would be a most serious thing to do. Some change was needed in thee matters mentioned by the other paragraphs, but he should certainly oppose the petition as a whole. Mr. tradshaw pointed out that voluntary effort provided two-thirds of the school accommodation, and the Board schools provided the remaining third; and yet those who supported the voluntary schools had to aid in keeping up the Board schools. He therefore thought the voluntary schools should have a share in the rates, and he would not object to the ratepayers seeing how the money was spent, hut they would not allow them to intefere with the teach- ing and the rest. The Chairman remarked that that office, the clerk, and the attendance officers existed as much for the denomina- tional schools as the Board schools, and the keeping up of that establishment formed a great part of the expenditure. Simms Cross School did not cost a farthing beyond the re- payment of the money borrowed to build it. Mr. Deacon also observed that fees were paid for children attending voluntary schools if they could not pay them. Dr. O'Keeffe said if the voluntary schools got a portion of the rate the money could be spent ender Government su- pervision in the same way as they spent the money that was given to them at present. The immense increase in the number of scholars was due to compulsion alone. Mr. Band having briefly replied, The petition was adopted by four votes to three, the Chairman, Mr. Deacon, and Mr. Wareing voted against the motion.

ECONOMY AND EFFICIENCY. The Chairman produced a memorial that had been for- warded to him, and which, he stated, had been signed by 150 ratepayers. The memorial stated that the high School Board rate pressed heavily upon all the property owners in the district. Economy held a very important place in the addresses of the gentleinen returned to the Board, and they now asked those members to practice that economy. They respectfully suggested that economy could be practised by reducing the salaries of the clerk and teachers, which, as they now stood, were believed to be excessive, and such as the ratepayers were unable to pay. It appeared strange to the memorialists that the salaries of teachers should be yearly increased, while in all the works of the district wages had been considerably reduced during the last few years. The Cluirman Paid the promises made by himself and his ccrileagnes were economy associated with efficiency, and he believed that efficiency was true economy. The enor- mous grants earned by the Board schools were the best proof that those schools were maaaged with efficiency and economy. If those schools were not efficient the grants would be reduced, and the ratepayers would have to pay very much more than they now paid. 'The teachers were not overpaid, and be believed were not paid more than those in the denominational schools. To reduce their sal- aries would he to lose a number of efficient men and would be far from an economical step. He would ask them to con- sider the status of the head master at Simms Cross schools. A gentlemen who could get the wonderful results which he obtained must be a man of great abilities, and must be an adept at teaching. He pointed out the !raining required for teaching, the know- ledge and skill necessary, and the exhaustion of brain caused by the work, and there were clerks in the works of the town, who were quite as well paid as the head teachers, • and whose labour e did not require faculties of a high order, and whose lives were much pleasanter than those of a teacher. He utterly denied that the wages of men of the statns of teachers had been reduced in the town, and pointed out that half the rates in the town were paid by the manu- facturers, who Deter sent their children to the Board schools and yet they had not complained of the rate being high, and he did not think the smaller ratepayers should do so. He had great Sympathy with many small ratepayers, because on the whole the rates were high, but that was always the case in a place where the roads, gas works, and waterworks had all to be provided in one generation. The. statement about trade being had was not altogether accurate. There was no lack of employment in the town, and he believed that the retail shopkeepers were getting excellent profits, and had not cense to complain of the rates. Mr. Bond said the salaries at his school were not so large as those Of the Board school. He was not an advocate for reduction, bat there was a superabundance a teachers in the country, and in future they should enter upon another contract with the teachers. The Quitman observed in answer to this that one of their teachers bed passed his clasa excellent-100 per cent.— and whose salary was recommended te be raised, was about to leave them because he had got a better place. This was strung proof that they were not paying them too much. Mr. Deacon showed that the salaries paid by the Board were not equal to those paid in many towns. Dr. O'Keefle thought the statements of the chairman and Mr. Deacon a sufficient reply to the memorial, which was pLaced on tliie table. FOOD FOR THE " CHICKS." Mt. S. Stringer wrote to the effect that it was proposed to give the "little chicks" a dinner on Christmas Day, and asked for the use of the Infant School at Sinfes Cross. His request was granted. INCREASE OF SALARIES. On the recommendation of the school management, the salaries of various teachers were increased acArding to the scale of the Board. The increase, which rang,ed from £9 to in, were equal to an annual sum of £154.

SPIRITUALISM V. CONJURING.

_ Sir,—After reading the letter from " Justice" in last week's " Examiner," I was surprised to see that he has found another excuse, for I thought I had prevented this in saying what my tests were. First he says that my accept- ance of the challenge was coupled aaith conditions which could be turned any way. When I explain my conditions and show that I will force nothing upon the medium but what is right, and, to guard against a second excuse as re- gards the medium's expenses, I propose an additional £lO to the sum which was first named by " Justice" (£5), but as I did not force this upon him, but left him his own pro- position to fall back upon (the £5 challenge), I am sur- prised to see that he has the impudence to say that I have to resort to gambling to prove my cause. But "Justice fr does not escape me so easy; I now publicly denounce Spiritual- ism as'an imposition, and professional mediums as impostors. Now let " Justice " or any other STA. itualist take this up and prosecute me if they dare we shall then have a chance of getting at the truth.—l am yours, &c., THOMAS ACTON. 99, Priestley-street, Warrington, Dec. 21st, 1886. f With this letter we must close the correspondence on this subject—for the present. As Mr. Acton's challenge hag not been accepted, we shall, of course, return him the £5 he deposited with us.—En. Ex.]

div.head: SLOUGH OF DESPOND.
div.p: THE SLOUGH OF DESPOND.

Sir,—l wish to direct the attention of our municipal re- Tr•entative (through the medium of your valuable paper) to the disgraceful state Hovle•street and the adjoining streets are in. These st-eets hsve been formed upwards of ten years, and daring that time, nothing whatever has been done to them in the sbane of drain:ng or paving, and at

„ present they are almost impassible. The quantity of mud . and filth that has accumulated there is abominable; you scarcely know in the day time how to avoid gettirg anhle deep in the dirt, if you have the misfortune to traverse any of those streets. It is a matter of surprise to me that we have been saved from some epidemic breaking out in this part of the town. My object in writir.g is to discover, if possible, who is responsible for this state of things. We have a medical officer of health and also inspectors of nuis- ances, whom I often 'see in various pasts of the town, but this part appears to receive no attention from them. We have also members of the Town Council living near, who must be aware of the condition of the place; yet, year after year is allowed to pass over, without seeing any im- provement to the place. One of these streets is named after the noble lord of Bew- sey Hall—Lilford-street. If he was to walk to the bottom of that street be would scarcely think it much of a compli- ment to himself that it should be designated with his name. Is it the owners of the oronerty or the Town Council that should see to this matter? Surely something might be done to imp-ave matters, if it were only the sending of scavengers to clear away the mud. If nothing else can be done in this matter I would suggest that the name plate be taken down fre the corner of Hoyle-street, and in its place should be painted in large let- ters, "The Slough of Despond.”—Yours, Sr.c. Warrington, Dec. 16, 1886. ANTI- DIRT. THE CAUSE OF THE IRISH REVOLT.

Sir,—Your readus may, or may not, weary of the Irish and their cause. However this may be it still remains that the Irish problem must be solved ere we can turn our atten- tion to matters nearer home urgently calling alike upon the people, and upon Parliament, for settlement. The story uf Ireland's wrongs is a pitiful one. Ontside of Russian and Turkish schemes for national aggrandise- ment, no parallel can be found to them. To the historical student, who may have at his fingers' end the woes of Po- land, and the troubles of the Hungarian patriot, the cause of Ireland's prqsent discontented state cannot fail to be deeply interesting. There seems, to the present writer, to be several peculiar leatures about the Home Rule discussion now so violently agitat:ng the nubile mind. It is impossible to suppose that the so-called Unionist Literals are deficient in the knowledge of Irish history. Take the Radical leader, Mr. Chamber- lain. Looking through his speeches, we find a depth of research and a vehemence of denunciation second to none of the Irish patriots. Speaking on the 17th of June, 1885, he said :—" I do not believe that the great majority of Eng- lishmen have the slightest conception of the system under which this free nation attempts to rule the sister island. It is a system that is founded on the bayonets of 30,f K.ll sol- diers encamped permanently as in a hostile country. It is a system as completely centralised anfi bureaucratic as that with which Russia governs Poland, or as that which pre- vailed in Venice under the Austrian rule. An Irishman at this moment cannot move a step, he cannot lift a finger in any parochial, municipal, or educational work without be- ing confronted with, interfered with, aed controlled by an English official appointed by a foreign Government, and without a shade or shadow of representative authority." Speaking again on July 6, 1886, he said:—" The Irish people enjoy all your liberties, all your freedom, everything which you prize, all that you find necessary to your ordinary exist- ence." To the right honourable gentleman and his sup- porters this may seem consistency; to the ordinary mind it is but the prevarication of an ambitions and disappointed wan.
With Lord Hartington the position is different. Born of a family, and belonging to a class, whose traditions and cute instincts cause them to look unon the sufferings of the

people with indifference, we have at rcely a right to be sarprised that at this all important and momentous crisis he lazily falls back into the arms of the bine blooded and ty- rannical class to which he belongs. I do not forget that Mr. Gladstone counts amongst his supporters a goodly number of the class have above denounced. There are those whose honesty of purpose may safely be depended upon, to go the full length of their knowledge of any given question. Asa proof of this I ask your readers to look through the list of names of gentlemen attending the recent Unionist Conference, and scarcely one Peer is to be found whose name is not identified with the Adullamite and dis- contented Cabals that have been formed during the past 20 years. Men who are connected with Leagues fob med to protect the "Rights of property " and perpetrate the Wrongs ef Men; men who have looked upon the maeLes with suspicion, and have refused them the title to every honest man's birthright—the franchise,—these are the men who to-day' are loudest in their denunciations of tbe who with tongue in cheek are chuckling at the gullibility of the English workingman, and are hoping to perpetuate a system that drives the I lab laborer hone his own native soil to compete with, a . reduce the weekly wages of, the English laborer. Of John Bright it is difficult to speak. No men better knows the worth of Mr. Gladstone, and ro man has :Token snore highly of his capabilities. Spe..kiat in April, 1867 he said ,—Who equals him in courage and fidelity to his Convictions? If they can point out any statesman who can add dignity and grandeur to the stature of Mr. Gladreone, lit them produce him. If these gentlemen who say they will not follow him have any one who is equal, let them Show him."

I ask now, who has placed before the English people the true causes of Irish discontent, in stronger language than these two gentlemen, Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamber- lain ? The educating power that has been at work for some time has accomplished its object with the party that has justly been called the "reading and thinking party," and we see as a result. that the Liberal discontents have to lean upon Tory votes, or else have, as in the case of Lord Hartington and Mr. P. Rylands, to receive the faint prair_s that is a thousandfold worse than the heartiest damning process which an honourable man conld possibly run the gauntlet of. Speak to the Litsral discontents of Ireland's wrongs, re- Mind them of Tory opposition to all remedial measures since ZBBl, and they confess it (Ili and clknowledge that Ireland

has been and is a down-trodden country. And yet, most strange to say, we see these men, shall I say blindly? tying themselves hand and foot, pledging to keep in power a mountebank whose speech and action have now become synonymous for waiting to "see which way the cat jumps." With the Tory opposition to Mr. Gladstone nothing need be said. They have got what they wanted—place. They made the Bradlaugh question the catspaw with which to irritate Mr. Gladstone, and when they got, not into power, but place, allowed the member for Northampton to take the oath, and would have allowed him or anyone else to take a hundred oaths if by that means they could keep on sipping the sweets of office, sipping it must be, so long as Lord Salisbury has to acknowledge himself in a minority. From this we see that the peculiarities of the position are numerous. First comes political party chicanry, that is hide-bound Toryism, next the self-seeking personality of Mr. Chamberlain ; then the social, selfish, aristocratic i 'privilege-seeking party, and last, but greater than all, the sentimental Unionists, all the discontents agreeing that the Unionist umbrella is large enough, and strong enough, to cover the whole heterogenous mass. ' Well, time which proves all things, will bring this to the test. The "Sentimental Unionists." I wonder; Mr. Editor, if it is possible for any of as to point out to these men that they are but seeking a INill-o'-the-Wisp. Like the federa- tion schemes one sees put forth, we are bound to look at them. I fear all are doomed to disappointment. " Oh," say these men, "why should Ireland be satisfied with the same laws that govern England ?" A very good reason can be given, sir. 'Tis a land question, and if any Unionist can say the English land laws are perfect, why let them say it, and then pr.ceed to prove it. I read that a Sussex land- lord has received no less than twenty-eight notices from tenants of their intention to quit their holdings. This is carrying out Lord Salisbury's argument. He says, speak- ing of the Irish tenant farmer, "They chose to obtain a statutory title under the Land Act, and under that Act their obligation is this, they are boand either to pay their rent or surrender their land." Sir, I contend that the doc- trine here laid down is unpatriotic in the extreme. Car- ried out to its legitimate length it would demand that the tenant shoula be possessed of the gift of foresight, when even the land courts have failed to fix a fair permane .t rent. No, the English farmer is simply a coward, and has not yet awakened to a knowledge of his rights, and of hl3 duties to his country. The Irish farmer, with a patriotism deserving of all commendation has determined to keep his farm. There is room for him ;he need not emigrate. He has also done what the English farmer has not the courage to do, he has decided on a "plan of campaign." In a fur- ther letter Ireland's claims shall be pleaded, with your per- mission.:
CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: EX AMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 25, 1886. LATEST NEWS.
div.p: THE EX AMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 25, 1886. LATEST NEWS.

threatened to result in the public calamity of their separating without a verdict. I have, I think, once or twice noted the tendency of English landowners to secure territory in the United States. They must hold land somewhere, and as the tendency of legislation in this country is to loosen their exclusive grip of their position, they have crossed the Atlantic in search of fresh woods and pastures new. Amongst British noblemen who have most largely yielded'to this allurement is the Duke of Sunderland. The Duke possesses large tracts of land in Florida, where he also owns com- manding shares in local railways. He has just set out to inspect his property, and goes about it in a princely way. His yacht has been sent to Charles- town, and the Duke, accompanied by a few friends, is now on his way to join it. Another member of the House of Commons who is just now conducting colossal transactions in land in America is Mr. Puleston, member fcr Devonport. Mr. Puleston is reported to have expended, doubtless on behalf of friends, half a million in the purchase of coal lands in Pennsylvania. Mr. Puleston, though , an Englishman, or rather a Welshman, spent many years of his life in Pennsylvania. He began his career as a reporter on a small paper in a village called Pittston,rapidly raising himself to a consider- able position in local politics. The announcement that the Queen will not open Parliament in person has caused an unreasonable amount or disappointment in Consefrative circles. For the last twelve years the Conservative party have been so much r ccustomed to look to the pres- tige of Vie Queen's preseace at the opening of Par- liaments under Tory auspices that they took it for granted the forthcoming occasion would be hon- oured as heretofore. It seemed the more probable since the event would take place in Jubilee year, when Her Majesty might be expected to make habitual effort to emerge from her seclusion. But the Queen not only will not open Parliament, but will not even stay at Windsor for the purpose of the ceremonial duties connected with the opening of Parliament. Thus Ministers, exceptionally over- loaded with work; will have to wend their way in wintry weather to distant Osborne for the Council at which the Queen's Speech is considered and ap- proved. This is particularly hard on Lord Salis- bury, who hates the sea, but who will neverthe- less have to cross the Solent in whatever weather may chance when the summons comes. One of the latest stories with respect to Mr. Glad- stone discovers him the possessor of considerable wealth. His income from land alone is put down at £14,000 a year, whilst he is reported to have something over half a million sterling in railway shares. I know no more of Mr. Gladstone's private affairs than does the writer of the paragraph al- luded to. But Ido happen to know that Mr. Glad- stone has no land at all. The Hawarden Castle estate was Mrs. Gladstone's dower, and the lord of the manor is not Mr. Gladstone, but the eldest son, William Henry. Like all other estates, the Elawar- den rent roll has been considerably diminished of late years by the necessary reductions made on the rents. A great deal of nonsense has been written about the cost of the Colin Campbell case. It is said the briefs were I,COO guineas with refreshers of IC3 a day. They were nothing of the sort. It is so easy to start this kind of sensational rumour, and no- body cares to contradict it. !Sir Charles Russell may have got that amount—l hear that he did, but I am sure none of the other silks received this mon- strous figure. The streets are flooded with illusra- ted editions of the trial. The likeness of Lord Colin is tolerably exact, but Lady Colin's don't in the least resemble her. Great efforts have been made tc procure and sell her portrait, but the working negative has not come to the surface. Mary Anderson has not gone back to America, nor is she "sojourning in Rome," as has been an- nounced. She is sojourning in Dover-street, Picca- dilly, and is to be met with constantly in the Bond- street shops. I believe that in September next she will re-open the Lyceum while Mr. Irving is spoil- ing the Americans and they are spoiling him. I hear she has commissioned Mr. Wills to write her a play, and that the subject selected has been the early life of Cleopatra. There is a report, too, that when Faust shows sign of exhaustion a Shakespeare revival will be put on. Mr. Irving seems to have given up playing lovers. He is gradually taking to old men's parts, perhaps wisely. It is understood the new revival will be Henry VIII. Perhaps so. Irving would be admirable as the Cardinal; but Miss Terry can scarcely be expected to concentrate her dramatic intensity on such a part as Queen Katherine, which has plenty of stately declamation, but not much warmth or tenderness.

THEFT BY A Paunut.--4ohn Crossland, an elderly man, who had been an inmate of the workhouse at Whiston, was charged at Preecot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. R. Pilkington and A. R. Gladstone, with stealing a coat, waistcoat, and trousers, from the Workhouse at Whis- ton. The prisoner was sent to gaol for ax weeks. RECITAL OF Mt:rm.—The third annual music recital by the pupils of Miss Quick, of Prescot, was given on Thursday evening in the new Assembly Hall, Kemble-street. Owing, no deubt, to the inclement state of the weather the attend- ance was not so good as on former occasions. There were about 70 pupils on the platform, and their varied costumes added brightness to the spacious ball. Taking the enter- tainment as a whole, Miss Quick must be coagratulated on the perfection of her pupils.

DI-FETING OF CONSERVATIVES —A meeting of the Con- servatives of Presc3t district was held in the Assembly- I rooms, Derby-street, on Friday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. William L. Evans, J.P. There were also present the Rev. T. Barnacle, Messrs. James Croston, J.P., W. J. Stewart, J. Johnson Brown, J. D. Banks, A. F. Evans, H. Cross, C. Spensley, William Evans, F. Green, T. Smith, Hall, Halsall, C. B. Johnson, William Lockwood, Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Arthur Evans, and Mrs. Banks. Mr A. B. Forwood, M.P., was announced to appear. He, however, sent the following letter to the secretary :—" Dear Sir,—lt was with much reluctance that I sent my wire to-day, say- ing a board being called for Friday I could not come to t res- cot. The meeting has reference to our Admiralty policy for next year, and I could not possibly absent myself with- out such dereliction of duty that my constituents would not approve.—Very truly yours, A. B. FORWOOD.— The Chairman moved that a cop of the following resolu- tion be sent to Mr. Forwood That this meeting. while regretting the inability of Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P. for the division of Orinskirk, to be present and deliver an address. desires to congratulate him on the position he had attained, and the satisfaction he has given to his constituents and to the Nation at large since his acceptance of the office of sec- retary to the Admiralty, and wish to express its unquali- fied confidence in her Majesty's Government." He spoke of the interest which was taken by Mr. Forwood in everything that affected his constituents, as was evident from the fact that he had been in Prescot for the purpose of consulting them as to what was desirable to do in reference to the sending of a deputation to the Board of Trade about the watchmakers' grievances. He said that an enormous number of watch cases were every year being brought to this countly and here' ball-marked, and be hoped that some action would be taken which would enable the English watchmakers to compete with their foreign rivals.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. John- son Brown, supported by Mr. Croston and Mr. Stewart, and carried amid applause.—Mr. Evans then vacated the chair, and his place was taken by Mr. J. D. Banks. Mr. J. J. Brown, on be' of the committee, then presented Mr. William L. Evans, who had been prominently identified with Conservatiern in the district, with a portrait of himself, painted by Mr. W. B. B3adle, of Liverpool. After Mr. W. L. Evans had returned thanks for the compliment, the meet- ing separated.

Mr. Chamberlain's numerous engagements prevent him from visiting Scotland until Easter. The Continental press continues to discuss most seriously tbe probabilities of war in Europe. An hotel at Kilkee, county Clare, has been burned down. The landlady, Miss O'Donnell, perished in the dimes. Viscount Cranbrook, in consideration of the agricultural depression, has permanently reduced the rents of his farms in Kent by 30 per cent. The rapid thaw, accompanied as it has been by a heavy and continuous rainfall, has resulted in extensive floods in various parts of the midland counties. Lord E. Cavendish is suffering from a severe attack of bronchitis, and was unable to leave Chatsworth on Thursday with the Duke of Devonshire, who has gone to biker Hall for Christmas. THE WOODFORD EVICTIONS.—TweIve young men were Indicted at the Sligo Assizes, on Thursday morning, for riot and resisting and obstructing the Sheriff of Galway in the eviction of James Broderick, at Woodford, in August. The evidence of the sheriff, Mr. Brady, R.M., and several police-constables was repeated. HEAVY GALE IN THE IRISH CHANNEL.—On Thursday morning the Irish express trains were seriously delayed by the storm in the Channel. A heavy gale commenced on Wednesday night. and the wind at midnight blew with the force of a hurricane. The high wind ' was accompanied by dense storms of hail and snow, and the cold was in- tense. SHOCKING SUICIDE NEAR CREWE.—Robert Cuming, a greengrocer in Crewe Market Hall, and residing at Hisling- ton, committed suicide on Thursday morning in a shocking manner. He was found in his stable by his little boy at ten o'clock, quite dead, his head being almost severed from his body. A new razor, with which he had inflicted the inju- ries, lay near the body. Deceased had only recently been married. ANOTHER FAMILY SUFFOCATED.—A somewhat similar oc- currence to that at Carrick-on-Suir on Monday, when a whole family was suffocated, was reported on Thursday from the village of Sonnaghmere, near Cloone, county Lei- trim. A man named Rogan, his wife, and infant and another child retired to rest. The night being very cold, a basin of lighted turf was placed in the room as a means of heat, and tbe door and window were closed so as to admit none of the chill air. Rogan's mother slept in another part of the house, and on entering the room next morning she found all four occupants had been suffecated.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

EXTENSIVE LARCESIES.— tlthe Present Petty Setsions,on Tuesday, before Messrs. R. Pilkitvton and A. R. Gladstone, a man ard his wife named Robert and Bridget McGarry, of Johnson's-court, Sewell-street, Present, were charged with stealing ;eom the shop of Mr. E. V. Morton, Prescot, within the last three months, an overcoat, a jacket, some rugs, and a lot of other articles, valued altogether at 45s.—Mr. Mac- kenzie defended.—lt appeared that the female prisoner had several time.; visited the prosecutor's shop, and the articles mentioned ,vere missed at stated intervals.—P.S. Walker de- posed that he found the articles at the prisoner's house, the overcoat being worn by the male pr;soner.—Mr. Mackenzie addressed the Bench on behalf of the prisoners, and con- tended that the male prisoner did not know that the articles, if they bad been stolen, were stolen by his wife.—The male prisoner was charged, and Mrs. McGarry, who had been up twice before, was sentenced to two months' insprisonment. PRESCOT Pzrry SEssnoers —On Tuesday, before Messrs. R. Pilkington and A. R. Gladstone, Thomas Flatley was fined 103 and costs for being drunk and asleep in his trap at Present, on the 11th inst.—W. E. Coson, of Huyton, was summoned for the non-payment of £2 17s 5,1, owing by him as poor's rate, and as the defendant did not appear, an order for payment was made.—Samuel Ratcliffe, pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing a quantity of growing cab- bagee, valued at 6d, from a field at Whiston, the property of James Sumner, farmer, Dragon-lane. A fine of 20s, includ- ing costs, was imposed.—Fdward Evans was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on licensed premises, the Brook House Inn, Warringtnn-road, Whisten, and refusing to leave when requested, on the 4th inst.—George Davies, a young fellow, was charged with assaulting P.C. Davies. The defendant with some of his companions was in the beerhouse named, when the constable ordered the last named defendant (Evans) to leave. Without any provocation defendant rose and struck the constable a blow on the eye. The whole of the company then set upon the conetable, knocking him to the floor and taking his truncheon, which was afterwards brought to him by some person. Defendant, who pleaded not gullty, was fined 20s and costs, or in default of ray- ment one month's imprisonment.

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—Tha monthly meeting of the members of the Board was held on Monday night. There ware present Mr. W. L. Evans (chairman), Messra, Golds- worth and Spencely, with Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Lloyd (school attendance officer).—Arrears of School Fees: Mr. Goldsworth reported, with reference to the %inject off of the arrears, which was referred to the Attendance Committee, that the teachers, at a meeting of that committee, submitted lists of the arrears, showing those which were recoverable and those which were irrecoverable ; but the commiti.ee thought that the lists were not as well analysed as they might he, and they referred them 1- ck to the teachers to make the necessary amendments —The Clerk said the amended lists were submitted by the teachers, and he now Produced them.—The Chairman suggested that the matter should come before a meeting of the whole Board during the holidays, and then they would be able to commence the year with a clean book—This sugg,stion was agreed to.— Schcol Attendance Officer's Report: Mr, Lloyd (school at- tendance officer) reported as follows:—" I have to report that since your last meeting I have visited the parents of 327 children, who have been absent or irregular in their at- tendance at the schools in my district. Notivs to appear before your Attendance Committee have been served on the parents of six children, and one summons has been ordered in the event of the boy not attending school more regularly." —The Chairman : Only one summons in the month. That is satisfactory.—School Requisites: A. small list of school requisites was submitted by the teachers, and they were ordered to be purchased.—This was the principal busi- ness.

PRESCOT CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH AND SUNDAY ScHoot..—The teachers and friends of these institutions met on Thursday evening in the schoolroom for the purpose of bidding farewell to Mr. Pownall, who has been an active member of the Congregational cause in Prescot for up- wards of 20 years, aad latterly holding the positios as teacher of the first male class. About 40 persons partook of tea, and the number Was considerably augmented at the meeting afterwards. Mr. Peter Chorley (the senior super- intendent) in the name of the teachers and congregation, presented Mr. Pownall with a purse of gold, which was gratefully ocknowledged by the recipient.—Mr. John Haigh (on behalf pf the class) desired Mr. PownalPs acceptance of a handsome'writing desk with a suitable inscription. The Rev. James Johnston supported the presentations and alluded to the honourable self-denial of teache-s, the wide influence of Sunday schools throughout the land, and their necessary permanence in the religions life of the nation. The following entertainment was given :Pianoforte solos, Miss Harris- song, "Good old friends," Miss Abbott ; song." The minstrel boy," Mr. James Woods; song. " I heard a spirit sing," Miss A. Dickinson ; flute solo, Mr. F. Berlow ; song, "J, yarn," Mr. Mercer ; song. "Tired," sM. Ha-ris ; : ' 7-td-bye." Mi. 9 Abbott; s "The vacant chair," . r. James Woods: flute solo, Mr. F. Barlow ; recitation, "Timothy Spot," Mr. Dickinson ; song, "Strangers yet," Miss M. Harris ; song, "Anchored," Mr. H. Mercer ; song, "Heavenwards," Mies A. Dickin- son. The pianoforte accompanists were Misses Harris and Seddon.. Mr. Haigh moved, Mr. John Beesley seconded, and Mr. Dickinson supported a vote of thanks to all who had contributed to the evening's enjoyment.

BARRISTERS—wbose professional labours. necessitate long in- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilaratm7, romforting, and capable of sustainin: exhausted natu,e as Cadbury's Cocoa guaranteed absolutely pure. Beware oX imitations.—Advt.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

PRESENTATION TO A SCHOOLMISTRESS. On; Tuesday the children attending St. Mary's Girls' School, Bank Quay, presented the mistress, Miss Jane Wilson, with a •handsome silver teapot, as a mark of respect, on the occasion of her marriage. The presentatien was made by 3fiss Parkinson. ACCIDENT.—Mr. Shillcock, landlord of the Bay Horse Inn, Winwick-street, met with a serious acci- dent on Saturday. He was summoned to serve on a coroner's jury, and, as he was going to a house in Tanners-lane, to view the body, he fell, in conse- quence of the slippery nature of the road, and dis- located his hip. He is progressing as favourably as can be expected. SPECIAL SERVICE AT WYCLIFFE.—At Wycliffe Congregatio al Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Yonge pr- rthed a special sermon to young women, his subject being, "Can a maid forget her orn-rr ents," Jeremiah ii, 32. There was a large coag gation. After the sermon a praise service w .s held, in the course of which solos were fidmir- ab-y sung by the Misses Roberts, Miss Podmore, Mr. G.Wallington and Mr. Pearson. The hymns, choruses, and anthems were exceedingly well rendered by the choir, the whole service indeed giving evidence of the ability and excellent training of those who took part in it. CHRISTMAS TREATS FOR THE POOR.—As the Mayor (Dr. Mackie) is, in consequence of his serious illness, unable to attend to public business, Mrs. Mackie has directed that 7001bs. of currant bread , shall be distributed on Christmas Day. Mr, George Riley, school attendance officer, has undertaken to issue the tickets, and the currant bread will be given away at the Drill Hall, between twelve and two o'clock on Christmas Day, at the same time as the hot-pot dinner which the ex-Mayor, Alderman Joseph Harrison, has kindly intimated his intention Of providing for some 500 deserving and necessitous people. WARRINGTON HA RRIEE.S. The r bove harriers had their usual cross-country run en Saturday, the following eight members taking part in it :—Walsh, R. Sherlock, G. Stokes, A. Ratcliffe, H. Maddock, J. Smith, J. Waterworth, and J. Chrimes. Owing to the ground being covered with snow, paper was6dis- pensed with. The harriers left the clubroom at 3-39, and rn along Swill ey-strtet to Sankey Green; then over Buttermilk Bridge along the canal to the right to Bewsey Lodge, then through the park on to the high road at the Limerick. Here they turned to the right, by the new read at Hallam, reaching the clubroom at 4-35, after a very pleasant, though hard run. Distarce about seven miles. HAYNES'S G-eat SaZe for only 21 Days is now on. Come early to semr.e hr gains.—Advt. ADMINISTRATION ORDERS.—At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, James Goodwin, a labourer at the Newton paper mill, applied to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes for an administration order. His average earning were ten shillings a week, and he had a wife and three children to support. He attributed his being in difficulties to bad health and sickness in his family. The application was ad- journed, as only one creditor was present.—James Swift, a labourer at the Vulcan Foundry, Earles- town, made a similar application. His earnings f3r the last nine months had averaged,a little over sixteen shillings a week; he was married, and had a family. The replies applicant gave to his Hon- our were not satisfactory, and his Honour said that as he appeared resolved not to. tell the truth, he should dismiss the application. AN UNHAPPY MARRIAGE.—A woman named Ann Ford, who was represented by Mr. Rideal, sum- moned John Ford, her husband, to the Borough Court on Monday, and asked the magistrates to order that he should contribute towards her main- tenance. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. Mr. Rideal, in laying his case before the magistrates, said that complainant was married in 1862. and, after having nine children, she was seven years ago deserted by her husband, who left her with five children. Since then defendant had been fined for assaulting his wife, .and was now living pith another woman. Mr. Browne said that defendant had great reason not to live with his wife, itS she was of drunken habits, spent his earnings in liquor, and, after having got him into debt, deserted him. lie also said that defendant alleged that she had sold two of the children to gipsies. The Bench or- dered defendant to pay 2s. 6d. towards the mainten- ance of his wife.

CHRTST CHURCH, LATCIIFOR,I).--On Saturday after- noon the annual sale of work in connedtion with this Church was opened in the Schools. Wash-lane, by Lady Greenall. All the stalls were well filled for the most part with plain and useful articles. The children's was a particularly interesting one, all the articles upon it having been made by the school children. The rooms were also given a sea- sonable and attractive appearance by a well-laden , Christmas tree, adorned with miniature flags, Chi- nese lanterns, &c. During the afternoon a play. I by the Rev. Canon Atkinson, M.A., Rector of Long- sight, entitled "Cinderella," was given in a Very creditable manner by the following boys and girls : —Cinderella-, Miss Annie May Bennion ; Altisidora and Dorothea (her sisters), Miss Francis Annie Chappell and Miss Agnes de Maine Gorton; fairy, Miss Kate Richardson ; Prince, Master William Dickens; Duke, Master William Wallace; and Lord Chamberlain, Master George Penketh Chappell. The music was supplied by Miss Jane Atkinson. Sale at HAYNES'S of tcooks and Sboes, to make room for w;nter gooh-42 and 44. Huroemarket-street.—Advt.

A DISPUTED CLAIM.—At Warihington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour, Judge Ffeulkes, William Eisen, of 125, Earle-street, Earles- town, sued Joseph Blakeinore, formerly of Salford, but now of Earlestown, for the sum of £9 Os 2d, for herb beer supplied to him in September, 1883, for services rendered by Mrs. Eisen, and for a set of harness. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. L. Riley for the defence. It appeared thai:, in September, 1835, defendant Blakemore pur- chased from plaintiff the business of a beverage manufacturer, which plaintiff had carried on at Earlesi:own, and the claim was made with regard to transactions that then took place between them. Defendant contended that he had been charged a halfpenny a gallon too much fo- sixty gallons of herb beer, and that the claim for the services bf Mrs. Elsen was a fictitious one; he also counter- claimed for £6 5s for corks alleged to have been il- legally detained.—His Honour, after hearing evid- ence on hoth sides, gave a Verdict for plaintiff for £8 ss, and disallow I the counter claim. THE GRAPPEN: ,t.LL ELECTION INQUIRY. The Local Government Board,writing in reference to the election of the Guardian for the township of Grap- penhall, in regard to which an inquiry was recently held by one of their inspectors, as to the validity of the election of Mr. A. Woods, state :—" We hereby determine that the said Alfred Woods was not duly elected, and has no right, by virtue of such alleged election, to act as the elective guardian of the poor of the said township. And we hereby order the said Alfred Woods forthwith to abstain from acting or attempting to act as guardian of the poor for the said township, under and by virtue of such alleged election as aforesaid. And we also hereby deter- mine that the said William Darbyshire was duly elected guardian of the poor for the said township, and is entitled. to act as such during the current period of office under and by virtue of such election as aforesaid." The letter was addressed to the Guar- dians of the Poor of the Warrington Union, the Overseers of the poor of the township of Grappen- hall, Alfred Woods, jeweller, of Garfield, Grappen- hall ; and Mr. William Darbyshire (the duly elected guardian), and " to all others whom it may concern.' WARRINGTON BENEVOLENT AND CHARITABLE INVESTIGATION SOCIETY.—This society, we under- stand, have taken the\ house No. 20, King-street, and have engaged\ the services of Sergeant Blease as inquiry officer and-custodian. The house is roomy, and will enable the committee to hold meetings,, establish sewing classes, and form a depot for the reception and distribution of left-off clgthina for grown-up people and children of both sexes, which mpy be sent to 20, King-street, and will be gratefully received. It is not the intention of the committee to usurp the functions of the Board of Guardians or Relieving Officers, or to interfere with the course of private benevolence, but they will undertake in- quiries into tie circumstances of anyone whose name may be submitted to them, and will endeav- our, little by little, to organise a system which will, by combining public and private charity, meet cases of sudden or unforeseen distress so .far as the means at their disposal enable them to do so. The society will also .administer such relief as they are able to do in urgent cases. Donations of all kinds will be thankftilly received by the Chairman (the ex-Mayor, Alderman Harrison), the vice-chairman (Mr. Roberi; Davies), or any of the 'members of the following committee :—The Revs. E. C. E.'Carletor , J. Drammcnd, R. Pilcher, S.Wilkrn3on, Father Sul_ ner, and J. Yonge ; Messrs. F. Monks, J. Smethurst, John White, and 11. Whitham ; Mrs. Allton, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. W. Dutton, Miss, Dutton, Mrs. Fox, Miss Clara J. Harvey, Mrs. Harrison, Miss Kendrick, Mrs. Litton, Mrs. Sylvanus Reynolds, Mrs. John White, and Mrs. Wilkinson. The office hours at King-street will, for the present, be from One to five o'clock p.m.

Every plir of Bogs at HAYNES'S greatly reduced in ir:ea —42 and 44, Horsemarket•street.—Advt WYCLIFFE COCKHEDGE MISSION.—On Sunday ve ntiengt beingtheß II Kings H . KWi.nR. preached gto a full congregation at Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission, the' sue n, b j text t oa ft some edilesncgotui4 jur. rsebeing r" Nreafaermr ea dn to onw explainedthh aat house of Rimmon, or holding a candle to the devil,' evening x he termed the modern houses of Rimmon, namely, the public houses, theatres and dancing rooms. He could not possibly see, he said, how a Christian could feel comfortable in a public house, the air and atmosphere not being congenial to his growth • in spiritual life. With regard to the theatre he not merely affirmed that it was wrong to do that Fhich was positively bad—what was considered wicked by universal consent—but he maintained that it - -as wrong to do that concerning which they had any misgiving—that which they only suspected to be evil. Rimmon had another house—the dancing room. The everlasting argument in favour of dancing was, "there is nothing wrong in dancing; we read of dancing in the bible." But it should be remembered that modern dancing is something t very different to the dancing they read of in the Bible. There were three things they should not forget, first, that bible dancing was all done in connection with religion; second, that it was all done in the day-time ; third, that it was not a mixed dance, males danced together and females danced together. He strongly advised fathers and mothers to keep their children away from modern dancing rooms. Having con- demned the opening of saps on Sundays which he said encouraged disorder and stood in Vie way of social reform, he referred to off licenses as a curse to their large towns. The passing of that measure had been a sad mistake and he strongly maintained that every Cluistian church ought to do its utmost to have it speedily repealed. After the sermon a solo "The beautiful city " was admir- ably sung by Mr. Farrar. DEATH FROM BURNS.—On Tuesday afternoon an inquest was held at the Three Pigeons Inn, Tan- ner's-lane, by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, as to the death of Mary Ann Dempsey, five years of lage, who died in consequence of severe burns.--Ann Dempsey said she was the wife of Michael Dempsey, who lives at 58, Tanner's-lane, and is a coal labourer. On Wednesday morning last week, abont 11 o'clocl , witness went to a pawnshop about 100 yards dig.- tant from her house, leaving the deceased and her brother, named Thomas, aged three years, in the house. She was away about five minutes and on the way back she was informed that her daughter hadbeen burned, and on a-riving home decePsee who was sitting in a chair, cried out "Oh, mothel., our Tom has burned me with a poker." She took deceased to the infirmary where she was attended to. Dr. Richmond wanted her to leave the child there, but as it cried to be taken with her, she took it home. The next day it died. The child had been . insured, but as the subscriptions had run out she had as yet received no money.—Patrick Hannion, labourer, spoke to having seen deceased run out of the house on fire. He put his apron around her and extinguished the flames, and afterwards cut her clothes off. The child was in his hands about ten minutes, and the mother was not there during that time. The Deputy-Coroner remarked that the witness, Hannion, deserved to be complimented on his promptitude and skill in putting out the burning clothing. He acted with great self confi- dence, and of course if anything would save a child's life under such circumstances it was smothering the fire.—Mr. Smethurst (foreman) on behalf of the jury, quite coincided in the remarks of the corone . —Emily Grounds, a widow, living in Tanner's-lane, said she hoard the child screaming, and on running out of her house she saw Hannion putting the fire of the clothing out.' When the clothes were taken off she noticed that' the child had been very badly burned. The Deputy-Coroner having remarked upon the fatal effects of burns upon children and even grown-up people, judging from his experience as a coroner, a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned, the jury, however, thinliing that the mother of the deceased should be censured for leav- ing her children alone in the house. Nrs Dempsey was afterwards called into the room and the Deputy-Coroner expressed to her the opinion of the jury. A CHRISTMAS PRESENT.-Fifty choice Cigars, in box, poet free, for 7s.—J. G. SAIOLI ET, Tobacconist, 19a, Sankey- sreet, Wartilgton.—Advt.
