div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

LONDON, THITEZDAY. Affairs in Ireland continue to give the *Govern- ment much disquiet. In some respects they are favourable. The number of outrages is considerably less than it has been at any time since 1880. Even the descent upon the campaigners and the arrest of Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien has not been followed by any popular outbreak. Anxious above all things to maintain the alliance of the Liberal party, (Ind confident in the issue of events, the Nationalists are content to bear their burden with whatever of patience is possible to them. The difficulty of the Government arises from within. Several Ministers, and a considerable section of the party, are inclined to follow Lord Randolph in his adoption of Home Rule policy in Ireland. On the other hand, there is an overwhelming numerical majority Who are for keeping to the old tracks and pursuing the bad old policy. These find encouragement in the daily howling of "The Times," which truculently threatens the Government with untold consequences if they flinch from the path of coercion. Between the two influences the Government are having a bad time of it, and the prospect is not likely to improve. It is understood that if occasion can be shown they will not shrink from introducing a Coercion Bill when Parliament meets. But I fancy the 'occasion will not present itself. The Irish members have made themselves acquainted with the bearing, of an im- portant fa or in the matter. That Lord Harting- ton and the Whig section of the Dissentient Liberals would support a coercion bill is certain enough. The question a week ago was what would Mr. Chamberlain do? The Parnellites have satisfied themselves through what they regard as reliable sources of information, that Mr. Chamberlain would, in such circumstances, join Lord Hartington in sup- porting the Government. As no embarassment would arise upon this point, I fancy the question of coercion will not arise in the coming session. The danger signal for the Government is hoisted on the Local' Government Bill. It is difficult to see how disaster can be avoided here. Angry pas- sions make men capable of many things, but even Mr. Chamberlain's personal animosity to Mr. Glad- stone cannot hurry him into the lobby in support of a Conservative Government proposing a Local Government Bill with fancy franchises and ex- officio members. But, after all, the Local Govern- ment Bill may not be reached next session. The procedure business will occupy much more time than is generally anticinated. We may have a war on the Continent, or half-a-dozen things may hap- pen to postpone the joining of issue on the ques- tion of local government. The committee whidh the Prince of Wales called to his aid to decide upon the particulars of the Im- perial Institute, have now concluded their labours. To-morrow some of the London papers will publish an official communique setting „h the conclusions arrived at. As your journal wil' not appear till the morning of that day I may, without breach of confi- dence, disclose the portentious secret with which members of the committee have been trembling through the week. The great point of difficulty was as to the site of the proposed building. It is no secret that the whole project has entirely failed in eliciting public enthusiasm. A dead set has been made against what is called the South Kensington gang, meaning the eminent scientific, literary, and commercial gentlemen who have had the pleasant task of directing the arrangemen..s with respect to the recent exhibitions at South Kensington. It has been plainly intimated that if South Kensington be selected as tl-e site for the new building the pub- lic will has e nothing to do with it, and its fail- ure is predestined. Well, the commhtee, not, I fancy, without fear and trembling, have resolved to recommend South Kensington as the site. They do this upon the ground that they have no choice. There is no site available in the city that might be had at a less expenditure than half a million ster- ling, and they reasonably urge that to saddle the institute at the outset with such a charge would be suicidal. What they .propose is to have the insti- tute located at South Kensington with kind of an- nexes in the city, nd in all the principal towns of the kingdom. The city and the boroughs will be expected to provide room for exhibits which will be freely supplied from the main soiree at South Kensington. I am afraid:the affair does not look very promising, but it must in fairness be admitted that the committee have been faced by circumstances of [treat difficulty, and have been literally driven to South Kensington. Everybody must be glad that the Campbell divorce case is over at last. Even the class of. per- son for whom the evening papers produce verbatim reports Must have grown sick of the monotony of its abominations. It was the openingof a drawing- room door in the highest circles of London society, and the moral at mosphere was found to be literally stifling. One satisfactory feature in the caL*s the unanimity of the approval which the verctif the jury has met with. It would have been a lament- able thing if they had been discharged without giv- a verdict, and a most melancholy one if, having decided upon a verdict, it had been an unsatisfac- tory one. Their conclusions are in each case the only ones that could have been arrivedrat upon the evidence, whilst the rider condemning General Butler has particularly satisfied the public sense of justice. That the General positively declined the entreaties of his friends and the commands of his counsel suggest only one alternative. What passed in the minds of the jury was shown by their hesi- tation in delivering their verdict. At one time it

div.head: RESIGNATION OF LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL.

"The Times" gives prominence to the following announcement :—Lord R. Churchill les resigned the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer. Our contemporaly understands that the imme- diate cause of his lordship's resignation was his un- willingness to burden the national finances with ' the sums deemed necessary by the Admiralty and War Office for the defence of the country. Lord R. Churchill considered th e estimates of the Se cretary for , War and the First Lord of the Admiralty to be ex- travagant, in view of existing financial difficulties, and no called for by the ,state of foreign affairs, but he failed to convince his two colleagues, who were supported in their demands by the authority of the Prime Minister. Sooner than place those estimates upon the Budget, the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer has resigned. It believes, moreover, that other circumstanc3s have combined in the past few weeks to make Lord R. Churchill regard his position in the Minis- try as a false one. He has not been satisfied with the shape which the legislative measures for Great Britain to be introduced next session have as- 8./toed after discussion in the Cabinet. They do not appear to him adequate to the requirements of the country. Commenting upon the above 'news, the "Times" says :—The resignation of Lord R. Churchill has, beyond all question, deprived the Government of its ablest member ic: we except the Prime Minister himself. It has consequently introduced a com- plete change in the political situation. The imme- diate problem with which Lord Salisbury has to deal is a simple one—ls it possible for him to go on with an Administration composed on the lines of the present one, but without Lord R. Churchill's aid? It is possible that Lord Salisbury may be con- tent with a mere stopgap as leader of the bower House, but if so he will deliberately run a risk which in the present state of Ireland and of foreign affairs ought not to_be faced unless for the most imperative reasons. In addition to objecting to the proposed increase in the army and navy expenditure, Lord R. Church- ill is at issue, it is stated, with the majorityof Cabi- net in reference to the mode of representation on which the new County Government Bill is founded, , and also in regard to An important provision in the new procedure proposals. His lordship will not give up possession of his office at the Treasury until his successor is appointed, but he was not in attend- ande on Th arsday, his private secretary, Mr. Moore, having at his lordship's desire proceeded to 2, Con- naught-place, with all correspondence requiring immediate attention. A great number of rumours are current as to the possible developments of the political situation, but these must as yet be accepted with great reserve. It is stated in some quarters that Lord Hartinp;ton may be asked to become Prime Minister, while in others likely to be well informed, it is believed Lord Salisbury will approach Lord Hartington with a view of the latter becoming leader of the House of Commons.

A Press Association correspondent. telegraphing from Loughrea, where Mr. Dillon, M.P., and other prominent Nationalists arrived on Thursday, says: —A bellman hasP been sent around the town an- nouncing the resignation of Lord Randolph Church- ill, and t he wildest enthusiasm is manifested.

SINGULAR SLIDING FATALITY .-0 n Wednesday Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at Gerard's Bridge, St. Helens, on the body of Patrick Skelly, fifteen years of age, 64 Victoria•street, who died after receiving injuries whilst sliding on a small sheet of water in Hardshaw-fields. The lad fell upon his head, and after reaching home lapsed into unconsciousness, and died notwithstanding medical atten- tion. A verdict of " Accidental death' was returned.

SIIDDEV DEATH AT EARLESTOWr. - On Wednesday morning William Gilligan, a collier, 20 years of age, who resided with his stepfather at 71 Legh-street, Earlestown, died very suddenly while in bed. The deceased, who ate a hearty supper on the previous night retired to bed, as usual, and slept with his step brother, a boy named Daniel Conroy, who is about nine years of age. Sometime during the night the latter was awakened by the deceased throwing his arms across him. Immediately afterwards the deceased sat up in bed and inaudibly muttered some words. He lay down again, and the boy heard a " gurgling " noise in his throat. The deceased then apparently fell asleep. Shortly after 4 o'clock in the morning a "knocker up "called at the house to awaken a lodger named Gilmore, who attempted to awake the deceased. He, however, found that the poor fellow was dead, though his body was quite warm. Dr. Patterson, who was sent for, expressed the opinion that death had resulted from an apoplectic serzure.

THE SHOCKING FATALITY AT RAINPORD JUNCTION.— Mr. Brighome, county -coroner, held an inquest on Friday, at the Junction Hotel, Rainford, on the body of James Grim- shaw, aged sixtt-six, a day wageman at Rainford Colliery, living at 102, Crawford-viliage, Upholland, who was killed at Rainford Junction on the previous Wednesday evening. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitor's office, Lime-street, Liver- pool, appeared for the London and North-Western Railway Company; and Mr. Peck, solicitor, Wigan, appeared for the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company. It appeared from the evidence that deceased must have b2en returnin:); from his work along a footpath which crosses the railway at the end of the London and North-Western platform, at the time the 4-45 train from St. Helens was coming into the station. The body of the deceased was found completely cut , in two immediately afterwards, lying part in the fourfoot and part in the cross-over points. The jury returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death," and presented "that the place where the deceased came by his death appears to be part of a public footpath, and in their opinion the London and North-Western Company ought to make provision for the bitter protection of the same."
